#10021. Residential Proxies Detected on White House Network

Our Residential Proxy Observatory, launched earlier this week, is a first-of-its-kind interface that gives researchers a global view of residential proxy and anonymized internet activity.

While our team was looking through it, we noticed residential proxy exit activity on AS2650. AS2650 is registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network. Residential proxy services sell access to everyday devices, letting customers send traffic through them so it appears to come from that device's network.

To make sure this was not a fluke, we checked these addresses against other residential proxy detection services, such as Spur and Synthient. Their public IP context pages independently identify these addresses as residential proxy exits.

This is public access. Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.

Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning. That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them.

Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement. This is how past botnets have spread. In A Broken System Fueling Botnets, the researchers at Synthient documented how the Kimwolf botnet reached at least 2 million devices, mostly Android devices with an exposed ADB service, through residential proxy networks. If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.

The White House is not the only surprise in the observatory. Residential proxies also reach some of the most isolated places on the planet.

Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha is the South Atlantic territory that includes the most remote inhabited island in the world. We recorded 413 addresses and more than 32,000 observations there, split between Starlink and the island's local internet provider, Sure Saint Helena.

We also recorded three observations from Antarctica. All of them come from a Cloudflare WARP address that points to McMurdo Station.

Residential proxies have infected every corner of the world, and it looks like there is no place they cannot reach. Layer3 Intel tracks residential proxy and anonymization infrastructure worldwide. Even when the proxies hide in networks on the farthest corners of the planet, we can still observe them, leaving threat actors no place to hide.

#10020. AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Microsoft's Project Perception adds Guardian Agents to monitor and contain anomalous AI agents, but experts warn that policing unpredictable agents with other agents may compound — not contain — the risk.

Microsoft wants security teams to treat artificial intelligence (AI) agents like they treat employees with privileged access: insiders who can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised.

Earlier this week, the software giant introduced new capabilities to Project Perception, enabling it to discover agents running within an organization, assign an identity and permissions to each agent, and continuously score each organization's risk. When an anomalous agent is discovered in the organization's environment — a problem that Microsoft describes as the "agentic insider" — Project Perception can now cut off the agent's access.

The first release of Project Perception, made available in public preview through Microsoft Defender in August, was designed to defend against AI-driven attacks. Focused on Microsoft's security operations center threat and investigation scenarios, it coordinates red agents to scan for attacker paths, blue agents to identify the greatest risks, and green agents to mitigate threats. Project Perception's initial use was vulnerability management, through MDASH, Microsoft's AI code scanner, which is still in preview. MDASH uses several AI models, including MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, the company's first cybersecurity-specialized model.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

"We're expanding Perception so that we can go secure the AI insider," said Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, in a brief video accompanying the announcement.

To do that, Microsoft is adding what it calls Guardian Agents, which monitor the AI-based agents running across an organization and can contain them when they stray into unexpected behavior.

Today, many agents run with the permissions of the user who launched them or by invoking the user's credentials. Microsoft's approach separates the two, Microsoft said in a blog post detailing the new capabilities.

Nadim Abdo, corporate vice president for identity and network access, tells Dark Reading that the system gives every agent a distinct identity separate from the user's "and will ensure that the agent starts with no permissions at all, and only up-scopes to the permissions it needs to complete the task the user is asking it to do,"

Specifically, Microsoft said the new release can detect 35 more types of agents running locally on devices, bringing the total to 60, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. It also includes:

Extensions to Microsoft Entra Agent ID that can assign an identity to an agent that was never built to work with Entra.

Dynamic Agent Risk, a continuously updated score built from Entra, Defender, Intune, Purview, Sentinel, and signals from Global Secure Access, Microsoft’s security service edge (SSE) solution that unifies network access and identity protection.

Dynamic Conditional Access for agents, which can block writes while keeping reads, restrict network paths, revoke access, or stop an agent's runtime as risk rises.

Microsoft Execution Container (MXC), a sandbox that keeps credentials and security controls outside the agent's reach.

Related:RemoteThreat Bets Security Teams Need to Test What Happens After Defenses Fail

With Project Perception, Abdo describes an expense-approval agent that reads a malicious instruction hidden in an expense report.

"If someone got a prompt that convinced it to start to try to do wire transfers, we can actually watch it accessing a wire transfer system and say, 'Wait a second, that has nothing to do with the intent,' and that raises its risk," he says.

Microsoft says it can act on rising risk immediately, interrupting an agent's live session, network connection, or runtime without disrupting the user's own work, though those are vendor-stated capabilities in preview.

Project Perception has an expanded agent registry that now shows up across the Microsoft 365 admin center, Defender, Entra, Intune, Purview, and a new Perception Agent Insights view. And Dynamic Agent Risk replaces previously siloed risk scores.

Related:Deception by Design: CISA's Guide to Tricking Cybercriminals

The controls themselves sit outside the agents they watch.

"The first thing [an attacker will] do is they'll manipulate the security controls," Abdo says, so the credentials and monitoring tools run outside the container.

Perception and Agent 365, Microsoft's control plane for governing that was introduced last year and made generally available since May, "need to be battle tested," acknowledged Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella during a fireside chat with Gallot during a CISO conference last week at Microsoft's Redmond, Wash., headquarters. He also admitted that Microsoft's own detection must improve.

"If I look at the state of the art of behavioral monitoring of, let's say, Defender, it has to go way up," he said.

Gallot framed the risk in terms of how models behave.

"Those models have proven to be unpredictable," she said. "They'll do anything they can to get from point A to point B, and what they do may not be what you intend them to do."

Much of what Microsoft describes echoes what other vendors announced in recent weeks. Okta's Agent Gateway separates an agent's permissions from those of the user directing it, and Okta plans a kill switch that would reject tokens already issued to a deactivated agent. Teleport, backed by Cisco, ties privileges to tasks so they disappear when the work ends. CrowdStrike announced an Agentic Identity Provider and Falcon Guardian, which discovers agents and controls that may run on Windows, macOS, and Linux endpoints.

Abdo argues that each vendor sees only part of the picture.

"If you're primarily an identity vendor or primarily a network vendor or primarily an endpoint vendor, that lens gives you some visibility to what agents are doing, but you need to have the other components as well," he says.

Microsoft's advantage, he adds, is that Entra, Defender, and Intune are already widely deployed and integrated, so customers aren't "having to string these things together from multiple vendors."

Microsoft says it will also take in signals from third-party security products. Partners can already publish agent risk events into Agent 365 through public APIs, Abdo says, though he could not yet name which partner integrations are public.

Forrester principal security and risk management analyst Andras Cser is skeptical.

"Most of Microsoft's integration with third-party players, especially in security, has not been first rate so far," Cser says. Because Microsoft has most of the products it needs in its own ecosystem, he adds, it is "interested in pushing its own products."

The question is whether that approach fits environments where agents run across AWS, Google Cloud, Salesforce, and ServiceNow. Last month, Okta announced the formation of the Blueprint Alliance with AWS, CrowdStrike, Google Cloud, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Zscaler to develop a shared architecture for securing agents across vendors.

Microsoft is not among the named members. Asked whether it would participate, Abdo said Entra has "always been built on open standards" and that "we're always exploring those things."

Okta, which formed the alliance, argues that no single vendor sees enough.

"No one company can secure agents alone," said CEO and co-founder Todd McKinnon in his keynote at Oktane, the company’s annual conference, last month.

Reacting to this week’s Project Perception launch, Harish Peri, Okta's senior vice president and general manager of AI security, says, "Microsoft's Guardian Agents feature will only be as good as the broader ecosystem it plugs into. If you want to catch intent drift in real time, you need signals pulling from your entire stack, not just one vendor's cloud."

Nevertheless, Peri echoes Nadella's framing. Because agents must be allowed to behave unpredictably to be useful, "we can't secure agents by trying to control how their models think," Peri says. "We need to control their authority."

The answer, Peri says, is "deeper interoperability and cross-vendor signal sharing built on open standards."

Cser interprets the Blueprint Alliance as "more of a partnership kind of map" than a true standard. Cser believes vendor-specific efforts like this alliance are "a marketing ploy" that tend to fade within a year or two. Enterprises need open standards any vendor can implement, he says.

Consequently, that leaves CISOs with an imperfect choice in what Cser calls "still a very fluid market." The current choices, he says, are either a Microsoft-centric approach built mainly on Microsoft products or a multivendor approach with "many vendors, many price lists," where integration "is almost always a suspicious kind of promise."

Some security vendors agree that treating agents as insiders extends the long-standing zero-trust and least-privilege principles rather than replacing them.

Denis Calderone, CTO of Suzu Labs, says the most malicious behavior may never look like an agent straying from its task.

"Dynamic permissions scope what an agent can touch, but the worst outcomes happen inside the authorized envelope," he says.

Calderone points to July's OpenAI incident as evidence that agents can work against the systems watching them. More than 1,000 agents in a cyber evaluation coordinated to game the system grading them, some by faking tool calls, before roughly 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face, according to METR.

Further, Calderone has concerns about Guardian Agents, noting that they are agents themselves.

"Securing agents with agents means the Guardian Agents themselves are overprivileged actors that can be manipulated or compromised," he says.

Cser shares Calderone's concerns about Guardian Agents. An unpredictable agent watched by another unpredictable agent creates "non-deterministic nature squared," Cser says. "Most organizations today are very careful about bringing guardian agents into the mix."

Following Perception's July launch, Forrester principal analyst Allie Mellen urged organizations to enforce "least privilege and least agency," limiting not just what agents can access but what they can do on their own. Microsoft meets the first test but not yet the second, Cser says.

"It is least privilege, but I wouldn't go as far as describing it as least agency," he says, adding that some specialist vendors are further along.

While Perception itself is in public preview, the new Guardian Agent capabilities are in use only inside Microsoft and with "a small set of select customers." They will be expanding to more external customers this week and to broader preview rings over the next few months. Microsoft plans to say more at its annual Ignite conference next month.

Project Perception builds on the controls in Microsoft 365 E7, the $99-per-user-per-month suite that includes E5, Agent 365, and Entra Suite, which supply the signals and enforcement points that Perception relies on. Microsoft hasn't disclosed whether the new capabilities are included in E7, but Project Perception is priced based on consumption.

Cser expects the release to push customers toward E7.

"I would almost be sure that this is another kind of making people buy stuff in more expensive packages that they don't currently need but may need in future," he says.

By his estimate, E7 comes to about $1,200 per user per year at list price, or roughly $600 after typical volume discounts of 40% to 50%, which "can be prohibitively expensive for a lot of organizations."

Meanwhile, Calderone says organizations don't have to wait. He recommends inventorying every agent, including those running on developer machines. Each should be assigned its own identity and credentials set to expire, and each should require human approval for consequential actions.

"That work is free today," he says, "and it's the foundation every one of these Microsoft controls assumes you already have."

Jai Vijayan contributed reporting to this article.

Jeff has contributed to Dark Reading since 2022 and has written for Channel Futures for over five years. Before launching his freelance career, he was an editor at 1105 Media, where he served as editor-in-chief of Redmond magazine and contributed to its sister publications, including Redmond Channel Partner, Application Development Trends, and Virtualization Review.

Previously, Jeff held editorial roles at CMP Media’s CommunicationsWeek, InternetWeek, and VARBusiness. #10019. 'Stop dirty datacenters': Europe-wide protests planned demanding building moratorium

Curbing compute farms played a big part in recent US elections, now Euro activists are making their feelings known

Campaigners against datacenter expansion are planning two days of coordinated action across Europe on November 6 and 7, demanding an immediate moratorium on new large-scale developments.

Following the US midterm elections, where restrictions on massive AI server farms were prominent in the campaigns from candidates in both major parties, it's now Europe's turn. Over 100 groups across 15 European countries will protest the boom in bit barn building over the next couple of days.

As well as demonstrations, there will be public meetings, stalls, petitions, walking tours, cycle rides, poetry readings and other creative actions, the organizers say.

The coalition of groups has put up a website – stopdirtydatacentres.eu – with an interactive map allowing anyone to find information on the events taking place and where.

In the UK, there is a photocall planned at 8am on November 6 outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) in Whitehall Place in central London, but also a Community Day of Action the following day at London's Brick Lane, where a facility is planned on the site of the former Truman Brewery.

Also on November 7, there will be a "family event" at St Michaels & All Angels Church in Great Torrington, Devon, to highlight the massive 1.5 GW data campus and on-site battery energy storage that is planned for 850 acres of farmland near the town.

The planned actions are a response to growing concerns about the impact of the wave of new compute shed projects on local communities, public infrastructure, land, water and energy use, housing, jobs and the cost of living.

Such concerns won't have been helped by recent events, such as a Google subsidiary reportedly felling 250,000 trees illegally in Finland to clear the ground for a server hall.

The campaigners claim that governments, the European Union and the tech giants are gambling with the future by racing ahead with server farm developments without proper scrutiny of the environmental, democratic and social impacts they might have.

A recent report found that businesses and private-sector trade associations dominated meetings with UK ministers to discuss datacenters, while environmental groups didn't get a look-in.

Campaigners are calling for an immediate moratorium on new large-scale projects across Europe, until clear frameworks are in place to determine whether new facilities should be built and under what conditions, with proper scrutiny and meaningful public participation.

"Datacenter developers in the UK and Europe want to cash in on the AI goldrush whatever the consequences. But communities everywhere are fighting back, seeing through Big Tech's PR machine and calling this what it is – a massive grab of scarce land, water and power resources by Silicon Valley billionaires," said Oliver Hayes, Head of Campaigns at Global Action Plan (UK).

"With governments failing to answer very basic questions about how many datacenters we need, what for, where, and how pollution will be avoided, the only reasonable course of action is an immediate moratorium," he said in a supplied remark.

They are unlikely to get much sympathy from the British government, which has pegged its hopes for economic growth on AI and wants more bit barns built to fulfil this. It has already used its powers to overturn rejections of planning permission for server farm projects by local councils.

Omdia analyst Alan Howard argues that datacenters also became a convenient political target during the US campaigns.

"The datacenter industry took a big hit in the US midterm elections which is quite disappointing, but not that surprising," Howard told The Register.

"The anti-datacenter rhetoric accelerated 12 months ago and in the last six months skyrocketed. While there have been many catalysts to point our fingers at, datacenters turned into an opportunistic political football. To be blunt, there is no shortage of politicians willing to exploit any opportunity to win an election and the datacenter 'problem' showed up just at the right time for this election."

Planned actions across Europe include events in Ireland, Poland, Denmark, Finland, Spain, the Netherlands, France, and the UK. A march to the Scottish Parliament in Edinburgh is also pegged for the following weekend, November 14. ®

#10018. Multi-Vector (Late Interaction) Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v6.0 update, it gains a fourth model type: MultiVectorEncoder, for ColBERT-style late interaction retrieval. Any PyLate checkpoint and any Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint loads straight into it, and colpali-engine models for visual document retrieval can be used too, through the same familiar API you already use for dense, sparse, and reranker models.

Where a regular embedding model compresses a whole text into one vector, a multi-vector model keeps one vector per token and scores query against document with the MaxSim operator. That preserves token-level matching information that a single vector has to average away, which usually means stronger retrieval at the cost of a bigger index. It's also the state of the art for visual document retrieval, where a text query is matched against page images directly, with no OCR step in between.

In this blogpost, we'll show you how to use these models: loading the various checkpoint formats, encoding and scoring, plugging them into a search stack, running them on page images, and keeping the index affordable. Everything below runs on a plain pip install -U sentence-transformers.

This blog is about using multi-vector models. If you want to learn how to train them, see the companion Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers blogpost.

A dense embedding model reads a text and returns a single fixed-size vector. Everything the model noticed has to fit in those 384, 768, or 1024 numbers, and similarity is one dot product between two such summaries. This works remarkably well, but the compression is lossy in a specific way: a rare entity, an exact identifier, or one crucial clause in a long passage all have to compete for room in the same vector. A query with several requirements at once runs into the same wall. For "green sofa with wooden legs and rounded cushions", a single vector has to blend all four into one point, so a green sofa with the wrong legs ends up sitting close to the one you actually asked for.

A multi-vector model (also called a late-interaction or ColBERT-style model, after the ColBERT paper) skips that compression. It runs the same transformer, but instead of pooling the token embeddings into one vector, it projects each token embedding down to a small dimension (classically 128) and keeps all of them. A 9-token document becomes a 9x128 matrix, not a 1x128 vector.

The interaction between query and document is then deferred until scoring time, which is where the name "late interaction" comes from. A cross-encoder interacts early, with both texts going through the model together, which is accurate but leaves nothing to precompute, since every document has to be re-encoded for each new query. A bi-encoder, which is what the dense embedding model above is, barely interacts at all (one dot product between two finished summaries), and that is exactly what lets you encode a collection once and query it fast. Late interaction sits in between. Documents are still encoded independently and can be indexed offline, but scoring compares every query token against every document token, which leaves far more room for the two to interact.

Scoring uses MaxSim: for each query token, take its highest similarity against any document token, then sum those maxima across the query.

MaxSim(Q,D)=∑Qi∈Qmax⁡Dj∈DQi⋅Dj\text{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{Q_i \in Q} \max_{D_j \in D} Q_i \cdot D_jMaxSim(Q,D)=Qi​∈Q∑​Dj​∈Dmax​Qi​⋅Dj​

Because the token embeddings are L2-normalized, each of those dot products is a cosine similarity in [-1, 1], so the whole sum lands within [-num_query_tokens, num_query_tokens].

You can read the operator as a soft alignment, where every query token points at the one document token that best explains it, and the score is how well the document supports the query overall.

The alignment doesn't have to be lexical, since the token embeddings are contextualized. Encode "Where do penguins live?" against "Penguins inhabit Antarctica." with lightonai/mLateOn and the query token live finds its best match on inhabit at 0.94, a word it shares no characters with! That is the thing lexical retrieval cannot do, BM25 and its relatives need the term itself, so synonyms and paraphrases slip past them. Dense embedding models bridge that gap as well, of course. What late interaction adds is that it does so without giving up the other direction. When an exact match is what matters (a product code, a surname, a function name), MaxSim still has that token sitting there on its own, where a single-vector model had to average it in with everything else. It isn't one-to-one either, since several query tokens routinely settle on the same document token.

You gain retrieval quality, particularly on queries where one specific piece of a document is what makes it relevant, on multi-requirement queries like the sofa above where each requirement gets to find its own evidence, and on out-of-domain data where a dense model's compression was tuned for a different distribution. That compression is learned from the training queries, so the model learns to keep what they needed and drop everything else, which may include exactly what your production queries ask about. The effect grows with document length, since more text has to fit in the same fixed vector.

The cost is index size. One vector per token instead of one vector per document is a lot more vectors, only partly offset by the smaller dimension. Encoding 4,874 Natural Questions passages with lightonai/LateOn produced 608,414 token vectors, an average of 124.8 per passage:

That's about 42x the storage of the MiniLM index, or 62 KiB per passage. However, indexes are often compressed, e.g. the same 608,414 vectors take 92 MB as a fast-plaid index, since PLAID stores a centroid id plus a quantized residual per vector rather than the vector itself. For scale, a 4096-dimensional dense model like Qwen3-Embedding-8B would need about 80 MB for these same 4,874 passages, so a compressed multi-vector index sits in the same territory as the dense indexes people already run. Token Pooling cuts the vector count before any of that, and Retrieve and Rerank avoids building an index at all.

PyLate comes up throughout this post, so here is the short version. Sentence Transformers handled dense and sparse models but not late interaction, so LightOn built PyLate on top of it to close that gap, adding the training, inference, and retrieval pieces these models need. Much of what you'll load below was trained with it, and LightOn built an ecosystem around it too, including fast-plaid, the late-interaction index that turns up in Indexing. With v6.0 those capabilities live in Sentence Transformers itself.

With the tradeoff in mind, let's get a model running.

Multi-vector models work with a plain install:

For ColPali-style visual document retrieval, you also need the image dependencies (see Installation for all extras, and Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models for multimodal support in general):

Sentence Transformers v6.0 requires transformers v5.x, torch 2.2+, and huggingface-hub v1.x. If you pin any of those lower, plan the upgrade first. See the Migration Guide for the full list of breaking changes.

Loading a multi-vector model looks exactly like loading any other Sentence Transformers model:

To find models that work, look for the multi-vector and sentence-transformers tags on the Hub. Any model with those tags loads with the line above, whether it started life as a PyLate checkpoint, a Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint, or a ColPali-family model for visual document retrieval. We're working through the ecosystem to get that tag onto every model that works, so the list keeps growing.

Underneath, MultiVectorEncoder reads each of the formats these checkpoints have been published in over the years, so PyLate and Stanford-NLP checkpoints load directly even where the tag hasn't been added yet:

Visual document retrieval models are the exception. ColPali-family checkpoints ship in colpali-engine's own format, which carries no information Sentence Transformers can use, so each one needs a small configuration added to its repository before it loads. Most of that work is done and waiting to be merged. See Supported Models for the current state and how to load them today.

Multi-vector models carry a handful of recipe knobs that differ per checkpoint: marker prefixes for queries and documents, length caps, whether queries are padded out with [MASK] tokens, and which tokens are skipped when scoring documents. All of them live in the module configs, so print(model) shows you exactly what you loaded. Here's the original ColBERTv2 checkpoint, which pads every query to exactly 32 tokens and truncates documents at 180:

That's the classic ColBERT pipeline: a Transformer producing contextualized token embeddings, a token-level Dense projecting each of them to 128 dimensions, a MultiVectorMask deciding which tokens count during scoring, and a token-level Normalize. Other checkpoints fill in different values. lightonai/GTE-ModernColBERT-v1 uses the same four modules with [Q] and [D] prompts, no query expansion, and caps of 48 and 300.

You rarely need to touch any of this, since every released checkpoint configures its own. It matters when you build a model from a bare backbone, which is covered in Creating Custom Models.

One value is worth checking against your own data, though. document_length truncates, so anything past it never reaches the index. For example, a 662-token passage through LateOn's cap of 300 comes back as 273 vectors, with the rest of the passage simply gone. Most of these checkpoints were trained on short passages, so if your chunks are longer than the cap, you can lift it for a single call with encode_document(..., processing_kwargs={"text": {"max_length": 512}}), keeping in mind that you would be running the model past the length it was trained on and that the index grows roughly in proportion. Multi-vector models tend to tolerate that well. On MLDR, a long-document retrieval benchmark, the multilingual siblings of the pair above show the gap clearly: mLateOn scores 77.92 against mDenseOn's 51.59.

Multi-vector models are asymmetric, so queries and documents go through different prefixes, different length caps, and different scoring masks. Unlike many dense models, where the two are interchangeable, encode_query() and encode_document() are required to get correct embeddings:

What you get back is a list of 2D tensors, one per input, each of shape (num_tokens, embedding_dim). Unlike dense embeddings, you can't stack these into one rectangular tensor, because every input has its own token count. The second document is longer than the first, so it comes back as a taller matrix.

Each call applies the model's own recipe for you. encode_query prepends the query marker, expands the query to a fixed length if the checkpoint asks for it, and caps it at the query length. encode_document prepends the document marker, caps at the document length, and drops any skiplisted tokens (punctuation, for most checkpoints) from the scoring mask.

The usual encode() arguments all still apply, so batch_size, show_progress_bar, convert_to_numpy, device, and multi-process pools work the way you'd expect:

model.similarity() computes the full all-pairs MaxSim matrix:

Mars wins, as it should, though the runners-up are close behind. Saturn also contains the literal phrase "the Red Planet", and Jupiter is a planet with a red spot, so a token-level operator has plenty to latch onto in all three. The ordering is what matters.

Scores often sit this close together, as GLInt shows by measuring the spread across a full candidate pool. MaxSim takes a maximum per query token, so a document will usually give every query token some decent best match, and scores start from a floor. Contextualized token embeddings are also anisotropic, clustering in a narrow cone rather than spreading out, so even arbitrary token pairs tend to score high.

There is also model.similarity_pairwise(), for when you already have matched pairs and just want the pair scores instead of the full similarity matrix:

MaxSim sums over query tokens, so its magnitude scales with how many query tokens there are, which means you can't compare scores across models with different query recipes. LateOn encodes the Red Planet query above as 12 tokens. Run that same query and those same documents through ColBERTv2, which pads and truncates every query to exactly 32 tokens, and the scores land in a completely different range:

Within one model the ordering is all you need, but if you want scores on a bounded scale, switch the model's similarity function to MeanMaxSim, which divides by the query token count. Back on LateOn:

Now every score is an average cosine similarity in [-1, 1], although you'll only see [0, 1] in practice.

If your corpus is small, exhaustive MaxSim over all of it is the simplest thing that works. Encode the corpus once, then score each query against everything:

Those 4,874 passages encoded in 20 seconds on an RTX 3090, and each search takes about 120ms end to end, most of that the MaxSim scoring against all 608,414 token vectors. This is exact, but it scales linearly in total corpus tokens and keeps every token vector in memory, so reach for it when you have a few thousand documents rather than a few million. The runnable version of this script is semantic_search.py.

Past that size you want a real late-interaction index, which Sentence Transformers doesn't ship. It doesn't need to, because these indexes store whatever encode_document produced, so you encode here and hand the token embeddings to something built for them. Indexing has working snippets for four of the options, and the section directly below covers how to skip the index entirely.

You can also get late-interaction quality without maintaining a late-interaction index, by using a multi-vector model as your reranker. A fast bi-encoder narrows a large corpus to a handful of candidates, then the multi-vector model rescores only those:

Only the 50 candidates are ever encoded as multi-vectors, so your index stays a normal dense index and the token vectors are transient. This is the same role a cross-encoder plays in a retrieve-and-rerank stack, but a multi-vector model is considerably cheaper per candidate. You encode the documents in one batch and score them with a matrix multiplication, instead of one forward pass per query-document pair. The runnable script is retrieve_rerank.py, which prints the timings of both stages.

Several vector databases index and score multi-vectors natively: Qdrant since v1.10, Weaviate since v1.29, Vespa for years now, LanceDB since v0.15.0, and VectorChord, which adds a MaxSim operator to Postgres that plain pgvector doesn't have. Milvus joined them in v2.6.4, under array-of-structs rather than the unrelated feature it calls multi-vector search. If you would rather not run a server at all, LightOn's fast-plaid is a pip install away and implements PLAID directly, and PyLate wraps it in a fuller retrieval stack.

A few others get you partway. OpenSearch and Elasticsearch can rescore candidates with MaxSim but not retrieve on it, and the Elasticsearch field is additionally in technical preview and Enterprise-tier. turbopuffer has late-interaction indexing in private beta.

The snippets below index text, but nothing in them is text-specific. encode_document hands back the same list of token-vector matrices whether the document was a passage, a page image, an audio clip, or a video, so the ColPali-style models from Visual Document Retrieval go into any of these unchanged. There are simply more vectors per document, which is what makes Token Pooling worth reaching for sooner there.

fast-plaid, Qdrant, Weaviate, and Vespa all take exactly what encode_document returns, so the code is the same up to the client library. Here's a working snippet for each, run against the 4,874 passages and 608,414 token vectors from the Semantic Search example. Each one carries the ingestion and query times it produced on one machine (RTX 3090, i7-13700K), with no tuning beyond what the code shows, to give a sense of the shape of the work. All four answer the query faster than the 98ms model.similarity took in that section, and three of them do it on the CPU, since fast-plaid is the only one here using the GPU.

All four returned the same three passages in the same order as the exhaustive PyTorch MaxSim earlier in this post, and the three databases reproduce its scores to four decimals! That is because their snippets score every document, which is affordable at this size and removes approximation as a variable. fast-plaid is approximate by design, so its scores differ slightly. The notes under each one say what changes when you switch to an approximate index, which is where rankings start to drift.

fast-plaid is LightOn's Rust implementation of PLAID, the index ColBERT was originally built around. There's no server to start, and it reads the tensors encode_document hands back without any conversion.

The index argument is a directory, not just a label, so the index is written to disk as it is built. Pointing a new FastPlaid at the same path reopens it for searching or for adding more documents, instead of rebuilding from the embeddings each time. On this corpus it occupies 92 MB, against 311.5 MB for the raw float32 vectors.

This is the only one of the four that is approximate, and it is the one place in this section where the scores do not match the exhaustive MaxSim. PLAID prunes with centroids and stores quantized residuals, so the three scores drift by a few hundredths in both directions against the 11.9192 / 11.7591 / 11.6710 computed earlier. The ranking is unaffected here, and that is the trade PLAID is making. It was designed for corpora far larger than this one, where scanning everything is not an option.

Qdrant needs a server: docker run -p 6333:6333 qdrant/qdrant. The client also has a local mode (QdrantClient(":memory:")) that needs no server, but it's a pure-Python reimplementation, so use it for trying things out rather than for timing them.

MAX_SIM is the only comparator Qdrant offers, and hnsw_config=HnswConfigDiff(m=0) is their recommendation for late-interaction fields, since the vectors are used for rescoring rather than graph traversal. Note that Qdrant themselves suggest reserving late interaction for reranking a few hundred candidates rather than scanning a whole collection, which is the Retrieve and Rerank pattern. At 4,874 documents the full scan costs 18ms and is exact, but that doesn't extrapolate.

Weaviate needs a server too: docker run -p 8080:8080 -p 50051:50051 cr.weaviate.io/semitechnologies/weaviate:1.34.0. Multi-vector support needs 1.29 or newer, and the embedded mode isn't available on Windows.

Defaults are enough here. Weaviate's dynamic ef resolves to 100 for a top-3 query, and this ranking is already exact from about 32 upward. That margin is a property of the embeddings rather than of Weaviate, so it's worth confirming on your own model instead of assuming the defaults hold.

Weaviate also supports MUVERA encoding, which made ingestion 3x faster and queries 1.8x faster in our test. It cost far more accuracy than that speed is worth at this size though, since the correct third passage didn't appear even in its top 50.

Vespa also runs in a container, but pyvespa starts it for you, so there's no separate docker run.

Vespa asks for the most upfront structure of the four, because you're declaring a ranking pipeline rather than just an index. In exchange you get to write MaxSim out as a tensor expression and see exactly what it computes. This version puts MaxSim in first-phase over where true, which scores all 4,874 documents and is why the output matches exhaustive MaxSim exactly. It's deliberately not what Vespa recommends at scale. Their ColBERT sample app stores int8-binarized vectors and moves MaxSim into second-phase to rerank a cheaper first stage.

Moving to that phased setup needs care, because second-phase rescores only the best 100 candidates by default, and here that window left two of the three correct passages unscored entirely. Raising rerank-count to cover your candidate set fixes that, though at this size the phased version still came out slower than simply scanning everything.

Late interaction is the state of the art for visual document retrieval, matching a text query against page images, with charts, tables, and layout intact, and no OCR step. This is what the ColPali family of models does, and those checkpoints load and run through the same API, with the revision pinning the open pull request that adds this one's Sentence Transformers configuration (Supported Models has the full list). Image documents are passed as URLs, local paths, or PIL images:

Each query retrieves its own page (the diagonal), and the second query separates much more cleanly than the first, since only one of the four pages is about outlay over time.

The code is unchanged. Underneath, the processor handles the visual prompt and the image patches, and MaxSim scores query text tokens against document image patches. A page holds many separate regions, which is exactly what makes late interaction a natural fit here, since a single vector would have to average a chart, a table, and three paragraphs into one summary. That fidelity costs index space, though. The shapes above are 755 token vectors for one page against 25 for the query, where a Natural Questions passage from earlier averaged about 125, so token pooling is worth reaching for earlier here than it is for text.

These are VLMs, so plan for the memory they need. The table in Supported Models runs from 252M to 8.8B parameters, and the small end of it stays practical on CPU where the multi-billion ones don't.

Page images are the common case, but they're not the only non-text modality. Sentence Transformers accepts text, images, audio, and video, and a checkpoint supports whichever of those its processor does, which model.modalities reports. A single document can combine modalities too, by passing a dict like {"text": ..., "image": ...} in place of a bare value. Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models covers multimodal models in Sentence Transformers more broadly, and the Usage documentation lists exactly which input formats each modality accepts.

vidore/colqwen-omni-v0.1 is built on Qwen2.5-Omni and takes all four modalities. Retrieving a recorded conversation with it is the same two calls as retrieving a page:

ColQwen-Omni was trained purely on image-text pairs, so its audio retrieval is zero-shot. It never heard a training example, and there is no transcription step anywhere in the pipeline. The query says nausea where the recording says carsickness, and it still picks the pharmacy conversation out of twenty by a wide margin.

Video works the same way, but sample the frames or it will eat your VRAM. Its release blogpost is blunt about this, that video "is very memory-intensive, so it's best suited for short clips":

At 1 fps and full resolution the same pair of videos produces 8,426 and 5,137 token vectors and peaks at 20.8 GB of VRAM, against 4,240 and 2,446 vectors and 12.5 GB here, for a model that occupies 9.0 GB on its own. The ranking is identical either way. Long audio wants the same treatment, and the release blogpost recommends 30-second chunks, which come to roughly 800 tokens each.

Because MaxSim is a sum of per-query-token maxima, a ranking decomposes exactly, so every point of a document's score belongs to one query token and one document token. That lets you answer "why did this rank here?" precisely, rather than by eye.

For image documents, sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.interpretability overlays that decomposition onto the page as the standard ColPali heatmap, either aggregated over the query or one map per query token. Asking "How much was spent on water resources and power?" against the outlays page from above, this is where the water token went:

heatmap.py is the runnable version, including the masking step that lines the document embedding up with the patch grid.

Text documents have no patch grid to overlay, but the same decomposition applies. text_similarity_map.py ranks a corpus and then attributes the top hit's score token by token, here on the Natural Questions corpus from earlier with the 32M-parameter mxbai-edge-colbert-v0-32m:

rich, mond, preliminary, and final matched themselves, while when settled on since and play on game. Three special tokens contribute 22.7% of the score while carrying none of the query's content. Below this table the script prints the passage itself, with the winning tokens highlighted in place.

If the index footprint worries you, the most effective knob is to store fewer token vectors. HierarchicalTokenPooling implements the token pooling technique from Clavié, Chaffin, and Adams by clustering each document's token vectors with Ward linkage on cosine distance and replacing each cluster with its mean, keeping roughly 1 / pool_factor of the tokens. Within one document a lot of token vectors end up close to each other, so much of what you drop is redundancy rather than signal:

There are three places to apply it, depending on when you want to pay for it:

By default, pooling applies to documents only, since queries are short and are the side you can't afford to distort. On the Natural Questions corpus from earlier, the reduction tracks pool_factor closely, and pooling all 608k token vectors took about 6 seconds:

A cluster mean is a worse match for a query token than the best of its members was, and the coarser the clusters, the more that shows. The original experiments measured that cost on BEIR and found very little of it, at 100.6% of the unpooled retrieval performance on average at pool_factor=2, and 99.0% at pool_factor=3. Halving your index for free is a good deal, so 2 is a reasonable place to start. How much it costs on your data is corpus-specific though, so measure it with an evaluator before you settle on a factor. The runnable comparison is token_pooling.py.

How far you can push pool_factor is also partly a property of the model. LightOn's hierarchical pooling regularization trains for exactly that, shaping the embedding space so pooling costs less and reporting 99.4% retention at 5x compression. Training with that regularizer isn't in Sentence Transformers yet, but the resulting checkpoints are ordinary PyLate models, so lightonai/LateOn-hpool-regularized loads and pools like any other.

Multi-vector models run through the same backend machinery as the rest of Sentence Transformers, so you get torch (default), onnx, and openvino, alongside half precision, Flash Attention, and torch.compile.

On GPU, fp16 with Flash Attention is the best configuration we measured, at 2.44x the throughput of fp32 with no measurable retrieval quality loss. Flash Attention helps multi-vector models more than most, because documents are only truncated and never padded to a shared length, so your batches have widely varying sequence lengths that unpadding can exploit:

Models with non-attend query expansion (attend=False, which covers the Stanford-NLP checkpoints like colbert-ir/colbertv2.0 and answerdotai/answerai-colbert-small-v1) reject Flash Attention at load time. Flash Attention strips attention_mask=0 positions, so the [MASK] expansion tokens that MaxSim scores would never receive an attention update. Use "sdpa" for those models.

On CPU, OpenVINO is your better bet where the architecture is supported, and int8 quantization buys a further speedup at a cost of about 0.4% accuracy. See Speeding up Inference for the full benchmark details, the export and quantization helpers, and a flowchart for picking a backend.

MultiVectorNanoBEIREvaluator runs the NanoBEIR suite of 13 small BEIR subsets with MaxSim scoring, and needs no data preparation on your side:

This also makes it easy to check the claim from the top of this post. lightonai/LateOn and lightonai/DenseOn were trained by LightOn on the same data with the same ModernBERT backbone and the same 149M parameters, differing only in whether they keep one vector per token or pool down to one per document. Running both over all 13 NanoBEIR datasets isolates what that choice buys:

Late interaction wins on 9 of the 13 datasets and on the mean, by roughly one NDCG point. The four it loses (ArguAna, FiQA2018, SCIDOCS, and SciFact) are the shape of the tradeoff you should expect, a real gain in retrieval quality at the same model size, paid for in index footprint, rather than a universal win on every dataset. The same pair scores 57.22 against 56.20 on the full 15-dataset BEIR, a comparable gap, so the margin is not an artifact of the small benchmark.

Alongside NanoBEIR, MultiVectorInformationRetrievalEvaluator, MultiVectorRerankingEvaluator, MultiVectorTripletEvaluator, and MultiVectorDistillationEvaluator cover the usual evaluation setups on your own data. They're documented in the Evaluation API Reference.

MultiVectorEncoder absorbs the modeling, inference, training, and evaluation of both libraries. Every PyLate checkpoint loads directly, and Supported Models lists the colpali-engine checkpoints along with the revision to pass where one is still needed. If you're migrating, these are the calls that change:

The difference worth knowing about is on bare (non-ColBERT) checkpoints, where PyLate's ColBERT("bert-base-uncased") applies the classic recipe by default while MultiVectorEncoder("bert-base-uncased") builds a plain stack, leaving the prefixes, query expansion, and skiplist as explicit choices. The training loss and evaluator equivalents, and the data-handling differences, are in the Migration Guide.

Save compatibility is one-way in every case. PyLate, Stanford-NLP ColBERT, and colpali-engine checkpoints all load into MultiVectorEncoder, but MultiVectorEncoder.save_pretrained output isn't loadable by any of them.

Models carrying the multi-vector and sentence-transformers tags on the Hub are the list that stays current, and we're working to get those tags onto every model that works. The tables below are what we test against directly, so treat them as a starting point rather than the full set. For text retrieval in particular, any PyLate or Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint loads whether or not it carries the tag yet.

Some entries need a small Sentence Transformers configuration added to their repository first, and several of those are still open pull requests at the time of writing. Where a revision is listed below, pass it until that pull request is merged, after which the plain model name is enough:

These load with their trained prefix tokens, query expansion, and punctuation skiplist recovered from the saved configuration.

The NanoBEIR column reports the mean NDCG@10 (higher is better) across the 13 NanoBEIR datasets, each a 50-query subsample of a BEIR dataset, as a fast proxy for English text retrieval quality. We used the MultiVectorNanoBEIREvaluator to compute the scores for the primarily-English models. A - means the model was not evaluated on it. Note that NanoBEIR is a small benchmark, and its scores aren't a substitute for evaluating on your own data, which is always the right way to pick a model.

ColPali-style models embed page images as documents and text as queries.

The NanoViDoRe column reports the mean NDCG@10 (higher is better) across NanoViDoRe v3, a compact visual document retrieval benchmark spanning 8 subsets (computer science, energy, finance in English and French, HR, industrial, pharmaceuticals, and physics). Like with NanoBEIR, NanoViDoRe is a small benchmark which shouldn't replace evaluation on your own data.

Most of these are LoRA adapter repositories, with the adapter applied directly onto its base at load time. Some also have a -merged sibling on the Hub (e.g. vidore/colpali-v1.3-merged) with the adapter already folded into the weights.

The three -hf entries are the transformers-native *ForRetrieval ports. They load without any configuration, but use more modeling from transformers and less from sentence_transformers. Generally, it's preferable to use the original models instead, as the ports score approximately the same.

Late interaction in Sentence Transformers rests on a lot of earlier work. Thanks to Omar Khattab and Matei Zaharia for ColBERT, which everything here descends from, and to the LightOn team (Antoine Chaffin, Raphael Sourty, Paulo Moura, and Amélie Chatelain) for PyLate and fast-plaid, which carried late interaction for years and shaped a good deal of the API described above.

Thanks to the ColPali team (Manuel Faysse, Hugues Sibille, Tony Wu, Bilel Omrani, Gautier Viaud, Céline Hudelot, and Pierre Colombo) for ColPali and colpali-engine, which brought late interaction to page images, and to Benjamin Clavié, Antoine Chaffin, and Griffin Adams for token pooling.

Thanks as well to the core MTEB team, Kenneth Enevoldsen and Roman Solomatin among many others, for MTEB and for the kind of hidden work that keeps information retrieval research running.

And thanks to everyone who trained and released the checkpoints in Supported Models. Without them this post would have had nothing to measure.

To learn how to train or finetune these models on your own data:

See the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers.

#10016. Cyber Insurance's New Reality: Underwriting Isn't Enough

Rising AI, social engineering, and cloud risks are pushing carriers beyond risk transfer and deeper into cybersecurity itself.

The relentless evolution of the threat landscape has pushed cyber insurance companies to follow suit with a continuous expansion of cybersecurity posture requirements as well as taking an active hand in the defense process.

While cyber insurance has existed for years, the ransomware boom of the late 2010s and early 2020s transformed it from a niche risk transfer product into a central component of many organizations' security strategies. Today, policies cover everything from incident response and business interruption to legal costs and, in some cases, ransomware payments. Some of the names you'll see pop up around this space include Coalition, Chubb, AXA XL, Cowbell, and Resilience.

The threat landscape, especially when discussing enterprises, was never moving at a slow pace. But compared to the business email compromise and conventional ransomware attacks of five or 10 years ago, techniques are now evolving faster than ever, meaning insurance agencies must work harder to keep up.

Related:What We Missed: Knicks Phishing Test Goes Out of Bounds

Large language models (LLMs) have enabled threat actors to orchestrate complex attacks, streamline malware and exploit development, design phishing lures without typos, and operate at a scale never before possible. AI introduces uncertainty into threat models built largely around ransomware and data extortion attacks, which insurers have accumulated years of claims data around. Social engineering advancements could alter both attack frequency and severity faster than historical loss data can account for.

While outside of AI, attackers are also coming up with new social engineering tactics all the time, and cloud resource consolidation means compromised credentials or a single stolen API key can lead to devastating consequences.

Thomas Pytel, vice president at Cowbell, tells Dark Reading his firm believes in underwriting that continuously adapts to risk. "AI is changing the speed, scale, and credibility of phishing and impersonation, so historical loss experience alone is insufficient. Underwriting must assess how a business verifies identities, authorizes payments, and controls its own use of AI," he says.

According to a 2025 report from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), cyber insurance premiums reached nearly $15 billion in 2024, up 7% year over year. Additionally, direct written premium (DWP) for the US market reached roughly $9.14 billion in 2024, compared with a market that was only a fraction of that size several years earlier. This underscores how cyber insurance has evolved to become a highly significant segment of the cyber-risk ecosystem.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

On the other hand, that same NAIC report cited nearly 50,000 claims across the US in 2024, the highest on record and a nearly 40% increase year over year. This could speak to the increasing number of customers choosing insurance, the aggressiveness of attackers, or both.

What remains to be seen is whether the industry's growth has outpaced its ability to accurately model the threat landscape.

Increasing insurance popularity also gave way to the rise of certain requirements for coverage, primarily demanding insurance customers uphold a certain quality of cybersecurity posture.

George Gerchow, IANS faculty and chief security officer at Bedrock Data, tells Dark Reading that a few years ago, these requirements were contained on a short form that "no one checked," but insurers now expect multifactor authentication (MFA), endpoint detection and response (EDR), immutable backups, and privileged access controls, while "some are moving to continuous telemetry instead of a once-a-year attestation."

Daniel Woods, head of emerging risks at Coalition, agrees. He says legacy underwriting models based on point-in-time questionnaires cannot keep pace, and this has been true since the ransomware epidemic took hold around 2020.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

This occurred amid concerns that organizations would use cyber insurance as a replacement for patching, practicing defense in depth, or using strong data and authentication controls.

Better posture may be an objective net good no matter where it comes from, though it also risks turning security into a compliance exercise. Gerchow says these requirements can feel like that depending on who you ask.

"Insurance did more to get MFA and EDR deployed in the mid-market than any of us standing on a stage, and that part worked," he says. "But the application is a snapshot, and too many teams treat passing it as the goal. The carrier finds the gap for you at claim time. Lapsed MFA or an untested backup you attested to is now one of the fastest ways to get a claim denied."

Jeremiah Grossman, CEO of cyber loss prevention vendor Root Evidence, says insurance carriers are requiring more to be implemented, steadily, year over year, and "it seems to be working well for many." However, he says, "The issue is that organizations tend to not have the data to properly measure and model their risk, and their carriers are often in a better position to do so."

One relatively recent development in this space has been the rise of insurance organizations as active participants in the security process. While insurers these days broadly require MFA, security products like EDR, managed detection and response (MDR), and validated backups, insurance firms will also offer security products and services directly to their customers.

Coalition's offering includes access to an automated detection and response product, for example, while Resilience offers risk management tooling and Cowbell offers services including risk assessment, penetration testing, and training. All of these firms also work with other security vendors to recommend preapproved products and incident response services. While on the other end, traditional security vendors like Arctic Wolf offer products specifically for insurability.

Coalition argues its "Active Insurance" model has resulted in 73% fewer claims than the industry average and is why 56% of claims reported in 2024 were resolved with no out-of-pocket expense to those insured. Woods says that as the threat landscape intensifies, insurers that passively issue policies and hope claims do not exceed premiums will face increasingly worse results.

"The solution is for insurers to bring threat researchers and security experts in-house to monitor the threat landscape and actively support customers in improving protections during the life cycle of their policies," he says. "Risk transfer is still a fundamental component of cyber insurance, but so is ongoing protection and prevention."

Some risk remains difficult to model. Gerchow argues that if a crisis were to occur tomorrow where a major cloud or identity provider was taken down or compromised, the market would struggle to absorb it, and, he says, "the carriers know it."

"Look at where policy language is moving: war exclusions applied to nation-state activity with no declared conflict, widespread-event carve-outs, and small sublimits for dependent business interruption. CrowdStrike in 2024 was a bad update with no attacker anywhere in it, and it still grounded flights and stalled hospitals in a single morning," he says. "A real compromise of a major identity provider means every downstream customer needs forensics, counsel, and notification at the same time. If I'm a CISO this week, I'm reading the systemic-event exclusions in my policy first and assuming a big piece of that loss stays with me."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#10015. Microsoft fixed Excel 2016 copy-paste bug. Then reintroduced it. Now it's fixed again

All of this has happened before. All of this will happen again. Maybe

The Excel copy-and-paste bug is back, which means Microsoft is making a second round of fixes.

The bug first appeared in the September update and manifested in multiple versions of Excel as a silent failure of the paste operation. Users copied content and attempted to paste it, but the destination cell was unchanged no matter how hard they mashed the Ctrl+V keys. Microsoft fixed it in mid-September. But it made a comeback in Excel 2016 when users installed October's security update.

Microsoft has now released a new build of Excel 2016 to address the reintroduction of the bug: build 16.0.5574.1006. The company wrote: "The new build includes all security updates for Microsoft Excel 2016, and also fixes the issue that was reintroduced in 16.0.5574.1005, in which paste operations might fail if the workbook contains conditional formatting."

Microsoft did not explain how the bug slipped back in. Copy and paste is, after all, a niche bit of functionality.

Users reported the recurrence of the bug in October after the KB5002934 update was applied. Rolling back the update resolved the problem until Windows Update pushed the patch again. KB5002934 is a security update that resolves glitches including remote code execution and information disclosure vulnerabilities.

The problem affects only Excel 2016 and is not the result of the latest Windows security update. Rather, it was reintroduced in an Excel update delivered through Windows Update. A user in a Microsoft Excel forum said the issue had appeared on workstations throughout their organization. "What's frustrating is that this is the same issue we encountered before, which was supposedly fixed in a previous update. Now it's back, barely a few weeks later."

And now, at least, it appears to be fixed once again. Still, if Microsoft is determined to reintroduce bugs into Excel, perhaps it might also be tempted to bring back the Hall of Tortured Souls (a secret first-person 3D mini-game hidden inside Microsoft Excel for Windows 95) and populate it with the testers who managed to miss the issue's resurrection. ®

InfoQ Homepage News Docker Urges Isolation and Governance for AI Agent Security

Nov 04, 2026 5 min read

Docker has published a guide to five security risks that arise when AI agents are allowed to browse, run code and call tools with limited human oversight. Writing with product manager Eric Jia, Docker principal product marketing manager Srini Sekaran argues that the autonomy that makes agents useful also makes conventional application security controls insufficient. The company positions isolation and governance, rather than model improvements alone, as the main defences.

The blog post identifies prompt injection, tool misuse and poisoning, excessive autonomy, credential exposure, and data exfiltration as the principal risks. Docker argues that these share a common cause: an agent can select tools at runtime, chain several actions together and often operate with the permissions of the person who started it.

Traditional web security often assumes requests arrive at known endpoints and are processed by deterministic code, but agents do not fit that model. A coding agent may read a file, install a dependency, alter configuration, run tests and push a commit after receiving one instruction. Docker says that a compromised or misdirected agent can therefore take a much wider range of actions than a conventional service.

Prompt injection is presented as the defining risk: rather than compromising a system directly, an attacker can place instructions in material an agent is asked to read, such as a web page, code comment, issue or document. Docker cites an incident in which a coding agent followed instructions hidden in repository content and performed actions its user had not requested.

The company is sceptical that prompt injection can be eliminated through instructions to the model, saying that an agent cannot reliably distinguish a legitimate instruction from an injected one. Its preferred response is to limit what a hijacked agent can reach, so that successful manipulation has a smaller effect.

Tools are the second area of concern. With agents use connectors, database queries, file operations and code execution to affect external systems, Docker warns that giving an agent more tools than a task requires enlarges the attack surface. It also warns that a tool description can carry hidden instructions that lead an agent to misuse the tool.

This aligns with guidance published by OWASP. In its Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations work, reported by InfoQ in September 2025, OWASP identified tool misuse as a major new threat. It described attackers manipulating agents into abusing authorised tools, potentially gaining unauthorised data access or manipulating systems while remaining within granted permissions. OWASP recommended access verification, behavioural monitoring, operational boundaries and tamper-resistant execution logs.

Docker's third risk is excessive autonomy. The post describes "YOLO mode", where every agent action is approved automatically, as a visible example of broad standing permission. It acknowledges that this mode can be productive, but argues that it should be used inside a boundary that prevents an agent from reaching systems or data it should not touch.

The company gives an example in which a developer asked a coding agent to clean an old repository. The agent generated an rm -rf command with a trailing ~/ and executed it without confirmation, deleting the developer's home directory. Docker also cites an AWS engineer who gave a coding agent a Cost Explorer bug while it ran with operator-level access. The agent chose to delete and rebuild the production environment, resulting in a thirteen-hour regional outage.

Credential handling is closely connected to that problem. Docker says agents should not inherit a developer's personal token, because every action then carries that person's full permissions. It recommends separate, short-lived credentials, injected at runtime and kept out of the conversation. Secrets in prompts, configuration files or image environment variables are also a risk, because injected instructions may be able to read them from the agent's context.

The final risk is data exfiltration. An agent with network access and sensitive information in its context may send that information to an unintended destination. Docker says the risk increases in multi-agent systems, where one agent passes work to another. It recommends allow-listed network egress and treating every handoff between agents as untrusted input.

Those recommendations echo other work covered by InfoQ. Google's GKE security blueprint, reported in July 2026, recommends GKE Sandbox, based on gVisor, for containing agents that execute generated code or call untrusted tools. It also uses Model Armor to inspect prompts and responses for injection attempts and sensitive data exposure. Earlier, Meta open sourced LlamaFirewall, which combines prompt-injection detection, reasoning checks and static analysis of generated code. Google DeepMind's CaMeL research, also covered by InfoQ, takes a different approach by tracking control and data flows around a model.

Docker's answer is Docker Sandboxes and AI Governance. Sandboxes run each agent in a disposable microVM with defined filesystem and network controls. AI Governance is intended to define and enforce which actions, tools and credentials an agent may use. The company says isolation is the highest-impact starting point, with governance providing oversight across a fleet of agents.

Community discussion suggests that isolation alone will not settle the design question. In a thread on r/AI_Agents, a commenter using the name HectaMan wrote that teams should first assess tenancy and risk models. They argued that Docker can be convenient but may still grant excessive authority, noting that it disables around 40 privileged system calls while leaving roughly 500 available. They recommended deny-by-default permissions, least authority, policy enforcement points and controlled information flow.

Another commenter, Groady, said Docker works well for personal agents on a local machine, but questioned a shared kernel when agents execute code on behalf of other people. They suggested microVMs or gVisor-based isolation for that case. The discussion indicates that the useful comparison is not simply container versus no container, but whether the isolation boundary matches the trust boundary of the workload.

Docker's guidance is a useful summary of a problem that is becoming more concrete as coding agents gain write access to repositories, cloud accounts and production systems. Its central claim is persuasive: security teams should assume that agent input may be hostile and design the surrounding system so that a wrong decision cannot become a broad compromise. The harder work is deciding which permissions an agent genuinely needs, how those permissions expire, and who reviews the actions taken under them.
