#9954. 11 nanoseconds per word: Ridiculously Over-Optimizing Anagrams

A friend recently pointed out a new Word Ladder game variant: Find a path of mutations from a start word to an end word, where mutations can be single letter changes, single letter deletions or additions, or anagramming the word. It annoyed me (the paths involving anagrams can be wickedly hard to spot), so, naturally, I wrote a solver for it. And when the solver took over a second to run, I of course had to optimize it. Along the way, I found a fun trick for anagram indexing—fitting a collision-free prime-product identifier for every word in the dictionary into a single 64-bit integer—that I hadn't seen before (though the history of computing is long and Knuth probably noticed it in 1965).

For completeness, I should note that what I was interested in was finding all anagrams in a dictionary---if you just want to find anagrams of a specific word you can probably get away with a much simpler hash table design! We'll use all of the anagrams in the next post talking about solving the whole word ladder.

The two usual tricks for finding anagrams are to use either a letter-sorted permutation or a letter-count vector as a unique identifier for the letters in the word in an order-independent way:

and then run through the dictionary and insert items into a hash table based upon their letter count. In python-ish pseudocode:

Because I'd been feeling a little, uh, rusty in my coding lately, I decided to implement this all myself in Rust instead of yelling at an LLM to do it (this is a leetcode-like problem so it would have done it trivially). That code looked like:

Using the Scrabble(tm) dictionary pre-read into memory, this function produces the anagram dictionary in:

That seems fine. Oh wait, just kidding, that's INSANELY SLOW. The dictionary has 178,690 entries in it, which means we're spending 173 nanoseconds per word to build up this dictionary. In 173 nanoseconds you could execute roughly 4400 instructions on my Macbook Pro M1. Who has time to wait for that??

When optimizing, one of the first places to be suspicious is allocations, and this one has them in droves. Every word results in either the allocation of a Vec or an append to a Vec, which sometimes needs an allocation. Practically, there are about 161019 keys in the table, so that's 161k allocations (!!). Let's improve those by using a slightly more clever data structure, noting two things:

So we'll do two things: We'll find a way to store singleton items without needing a dynamic-length data structure at all, and we'll implement the equivalent of a linked list for appending items to the lists, since they're append-only and we only scan them once at the end. To do this, we'll use a structure like this:

Where heads is indexed by the anagram-identifying-key (e.g., the character-sorted string). We'll overload that u32 by using the high bit (we only have 170k or so words) to let it represent either an actual data value (the index of an element in the list) OR an index into the next+word arrays. The next array is our linked list - it stores pointers to another entry in the next array. The word array stores the associated data. It looks like this:

Much better, but we can do better yet. The time to sort that string and create a new string allocation is non-trivial and we're doing 178k of them. That's going to be another big chunk of nanoseconds.

Let's try a letter count vector instead, and pack it tightly into an integer. With only 26 characters, if we assume that no word has more than 15 repetitions of the same character, we could use 4 bits per character for 26 x 4=104 bits. That fits comfortably in a u128, and while that's not tiny, it's at least a nice fixed size 16 byte thing we can use as a fast hash table key.

(Note that we've done something else here - we're only returning the list of anagrams, not a full dictionary containing all of the words that don't have anagrams.)

Avoiding the string manipulation and sorting gives a big win:

At this point, we might ask a question like "how much does the slow default Rust hash table cost us?"

So we'll switch to the rustc_hash FxHashMap, which is much faster if you don't have to worry about adversarial inputs to your hash table.

That seems much better. But are we done yet?

Storing the letter count as a u128 is also a little slower than necessary, because it'll be split across two 64 bit registers and requires the compiler to carry that addition across them and do twice as much work for equality testing. But if we tried lettercounting in 64 bits, we would only be able to store 2 bits, and many words have more than 3 of the same letter ("MISSISSIPPI", for example, already has 4 S's).

Instead, we'll use an approach based on Gödel numbering: we'll create a small table associating one distinct prime number with each letter, and identify each word by the product of the letter-primes. This guarantees a unique identifier for each mix of letters. Naively, one might assign "a -> 2, b -> 3, c -> 5" and so on. But this is a practical blog post, and we'd like to fit the result in 64 bits; if we use the naive assignment, we overflow at the 365th word in our dictionary, "ABORTIVENESSES". And that's only 14 characters long, we have 3157 15-character words as well! If we let it wrap, we'll have just implemented a hash function, and there's no guarantee that two words won't accidentally collide, so then we'd need to add some machinery to check that...

So here's the trick: Find an optimized assignment of primes to letters in the alphabet such that none of the words in our Scrabble dictionary overflow a 64 bit number. I started out thinking about the standard English letter frequency (ETAOINSHRDLU, etc.), but that turns out to be a little wrong: We don't care much about words like "the", we care about words like "WRONGHEADEDNESS". So instead, we need to go based on the patterns found in the 3157 15-character words. In particular, while "E" remains assigned to 2, the common "T" is assigned 29, and we use 3 for "I". Our friend "J" is assigned 101, since the longest word with two or more J's in it is only 12 characters long: JEJUNENESSES. Looking at that, those E's and N's and S's better have low values, and they do: 2, 19, 17. We could handle 15 N's in a row in 64 bits still.

To solve this, I had a small program start with the letter-frequency ordering (which does a lot better than alphabetical but isn't good enough), loop finding the first word that overflowed and switch out some of its primes for lower valued primes. This would have also been fun to throw at a solver.

which doesn't overflow for any word in the Scrabble dictionary. We've found a collision-free canonical 64-bit identifier for the bag of letters in a (Scrabble) word, which looks like this in code:

In this representation, the largest product word is

which in log2 is 63.945; it's about 96.2% of the way through the 64 bit number space. Close, but it fits.

Result: 4.1ms -> 2.6ms (14.7ns / word — 12x faster than baseline)

And then there's a final optimization you can do: Instead of reading the dictionary into strings, read them into a packed u128 representation using 5 bits per character, and then add some instruction-level parallelism for our CPU (ILP) by doing the product accumulation using two independent accumulators. This u128 representation is useful for speeding up other parts of the word ladder solver later. That code looks like this:

Result: 2.6ms -> 2.3ms (13 ns/word - 13x faster than baseline)

This is looking pretty good. The only last optimization I have to add is to address some branch mispredictions in that rest != 0 loop. We can instead just treat all words as if they're 16 characters long and ignore the 0's at the end by mapping them to 1 in our primes table (i.e., they have no effect on the product). Using a fixed length of 16 also permits more auto-vectorization by our friendly compiler. To support that, we also separate the computation of the prime product from the insertion into the hash table, allowing more ILP from our now-vectorized multiplication loop.

Result: 2.3 ms -> 1.96ms (10.9ns/word, 15x faster than baseline)

We're finally pretty close to what I think a single core on my machine can get without explicit vectorization. That 1.96ms is about 1.23ns per byte, which could theoretically be about 3.2 x 8 x 1.23 = 31 instructions (but realistically fewer), which doesn't leave a ton of room for optimization---though I could be wrong! There's some space in there for an even faster hash table implementation but I'd rather stick with common, off-the-shelf things there.

In the next post I'll show how we solve the entire word ladder problem, using the anagrams we've found as a part of it.

#9953. Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.

That is embarrassing onstage. In production, it is a reliability problem: a workflow that succeeded once may fail the next time a user makes the same request. For mission-critical work, such as reconciling a financial transaction or checking a contract for an obligation, that can be a showstopper.

Most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average. On AppWorld, a ReAct agent using GPT-4.1 succeeded on 77.4% of runs across five repetitions. But it succeeded in all five runs for only 53.0% of tasks — a 24.4-point consistency gap.

Most benchmarks report the first number. We built a way to measure the second — and improve it.

In an earlier post, we introduced ALTK-Evolve — a system that turns an agent's own past trajectories into reusable guidelines, distilled automatically and injected back at inference time. It measurably improves task success, but those results only asked the average-case question too. This post introduces consistency guidelines, a new guideline type in altk-evolve built on top of a diagnostic tool we call the Consistency Analyzer, that targets this gap directly.

Standard agent evaluation reports Mean@k: run a benchmark k times, average the pass rate. Often k=3, sometimes just 1. It's the number on every leaderboard, and it's what "77% accurate" means in practice.

Mean@k answers "how good is this agent, on average?" It does not answer the question a real user cares about: will it still be good if I ask this exact question again? For that you need Pass^k: the fraction of tasks where the agent succeeds on all k runs.

⚠️ Pass^k is not Pass@k. The familiar Pass@k is optimistic — it asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeded, the right question when you can verify and retry. Pass^k is its pessimistic mirror image: every attempt must succeed. Same letters, opposite question. Pass^k ≤ Mean@k ≤ Pass@k, always.

A ReAct agent backed by GPT-4.1 posts a Mean@5 of 77.4% — genuinely strong. But Pass^5 is only 53.0%. Nearly a quarter of the benchmark consists of tasks the agent can sometimes solve and sometimes can't, with nothing about the task changing between runs. We call this gap — Mean@k minus Pass^k — the consistency gap.

This isn't a capability problem you fix with a bigger model. It's an orthogonal axis: an agent can be capable and inconsistent at the same time.

Every time an LLM agent decides something — which API to call, what argument to pass, whether to retry — that decision comes out of a probability distribution over next tokens. What matters is the shape of that distribution. A sharp one puts most of its mass on a single token: the runners-up are far behind, and the same choice comes out run after run. A flat one spreads comparable mass across several near-tied tokens, and which one wins is close to a coin flip.

The shape decides how much noise it takes to change the outcome. Sharp distributions are resilient — GPU floating-point non-associativity, request batching, and other platform-side effects nudge the numbers slightly, but nowhere near enough to reorder a clear winner. Flat distributions are vulnerable to exactly that nudge: near-ties may reorder under small perturbations. And because a trajectory chains dozens of decisions, a small per-step chance of flipping compounds into a large chance that some run goes differently. That's where a 24-point gap comes from.

This is also why the problem survives your decoding settings. Greedy decoding and a fixed seed both govern how a distribution gets turned into a token — they say nothing about the distribution itself. On a hosted endpoint the probabilities shift slightly from run to run, so the same prompt to the same model at temperature zero can still resolve a near-tie one way today and the other way tomorrow.

Our setup: the ReAct agent runs at temperature 0.0, so none of the variance above is ordinary sampling.

Which turns the problem into a search: which steps in a given trajectory were the flat ones — and what do you do about them once you know?

Consistency guidelines come out of a two-stage pipeline that plugs into ALTK-Evolve's existing machinery — with a new source signal driving what gets written.

1. Detect — the Consistency Analyzer. Given one recorded trajectory, the analyzer replays each decision step through controlled resampling, measuring how much the model's output actually varies at that point. Concretely, that's one additional model call per decision step, done once offline — issued with the sampling parameter set to draw k completions at once (k=5 by default) — replayed against the already-recorded context, not new tool calls, not new environment interactions, and not a second end-to-end rollout of the task. This yields a consistency score per decision step that is written into a scorecard to pinpoint exactly which decisions are at risk of flipping on the next run. Detection is fully black-box — no logits, no model internals, no instrumentation beyond the trace you already have.

2. Generate — targeted guidelines. Every flagged step becomes a candidate consistency guideline in the standard ALTK-Evolve format, so it slots into the existing storage and retrieval pipeline. Here's a real example, generated by GPT-4.1 from a trajectory of the AppWorld task "How many activities are done in my bucket list as per my SimpleNote note?":

[Guideline 1] When counting checkbox-style markers in note content, use a line-anchored regex match rather than a plain substring count — note titles often repeat the marker symbol in a legend line.

[Guideline 2] Always verify search results for note queries by checking for multiple matches and confirming the correct note before proceeding.

Nothing here is task-specific trivia. String-counting bugs and unverified search results are decision points that show up with high uncertainty across many AppWorld tasks. That's the point: the analyzer targets instability, not failure — so it catches steps the agent happened to get right this time but could easily get wrong next time.

Watch the 2-minute demo — five parallel runs of the agent split 3-2 on this task because of agent uncertainty about the counting strategy, then run again after these guidelines in context: all five agree.

We evaluated on AppWorld test_normal (168 tasks) with a ReAct agent on GPT-4.1, generating consistency guidelines from a single baseline trajectory per task and testing them on 5 fresh runs.

Mean@5 (%), aggregate — same scale as Pass^5 above.

The consistency gap is cut roughly in half. Aggregate Pass^5 rises 53.0% → 69.0% while Mean@5 rises 77.4% → 81.0%, narrowing the gap between "looks capable" and "can be counted on" from 24.4pp to 12.0pp. Nearly a third of previously-inconsistent tasks become tasks the agent passes on every single run.

The middle and hard tiers gain most. Medium +22.9pp (+44% relative), Hard +14.3pp (+45% relative) — effectively tied in relative terms, with Medium ahead absolutely. Easy gains +12.2pp, having had the least room. This is consistency guidelines doing what they're designed to do: finding and stabilizing the specific decision points where an agent's own uncertainty was leaking into the outcome.

Mean@5 never drops. Preserving average accuracy was a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have: a system that boosts Pass^5 by trading away Mean@5 would just be shifting unreliability around, not fixing it. Mean accuracy holds or improves at every difficulty level.

Applied to a different but related task in the same AppWorld scenario — another variant of the scenario the guidelines were mined from — consistency guidelines still lift Pass^5 by +13.0pp, only 3 points below the same-task number. A guideline derived from one run isn't just patching that run; it's capturing something that transfers.

The sharper evidence comes from a weaker model, gpt-oss-120b. Same-task Pass^5 rose +6.0pp from a much lower baseline (10.1% → 16.1%) — and, interestingly, the similar-task generalization number (+8.7 pp) actually exceeded the same-task gain, suggesting the guidelines were capturing genuinely reusable failure patterns rather than memorizing one trajectory's specifics.

Try the ALTK-Evolve — the open-source repo now includes the Consistency Analyzer and consistency-guideline generation used in these experiments — or read the technical report on arXiv for the complete methodology.

If accuracy numbers you can't reproduce on your own tasks sound familiar, we'd like to hear about it — concrete examples of flip-prone behavior in your own agents are exactly the kind of feedback that shapes what we build next. Open an issue or a discussion.

Great perspective on agent reliability. Measuring consistency alongside accuracy seems especially important as AI agents move into workflows where reproducibility matters. The Consistency Analyzer approach is a fascinating way to identify unstable decisions without requiring full task replays.

The useful split is the one most dashboards still refuse to print: Mean@k answers “how good is this agent on average?” Pass^k answers “will the same request still succeed if I ask again?”

Once you’ve watched a trajectory chain dozens of near-tied tool choices, a strong average with a wide consistency gap is exactly the demo that fails live. Capability and consistency are orthogonal — buying a bigger model can lift Mean without closing the gap.

What I want teams to take from the Consistency Analyzer framing is operational, not the guideline machinery itself: treat flip-prone decision steps as first-class eval targets. One offline resample pass over a recorded trace is a cheaper reliability signal than another end-to-end leaderboard screenshot.

Practical ask for anyone shipping agents from this: do you report Pass^k (even k=3) next to Mean@k in the release gate, and do you refuse the “stable” label when the consistency gap is still large on your hard tier?

Reproducible reliability will not remove disagreement about which guidelines to inject. It will make the disagreement about the right metric.

Thanks, and you've landed on exactly the operational takeaway we hoped for: flip-prone decision steps should be eval targets in their own right. Beyond that, knowing where they are also turns the eval into a diagnostic: a consistency gap tells you that an agent is unreliable, while the flip-prone steps tell you where and why.

On your release-gate question: we'd strongly encourage it, and k=3 is a sensible default. A few things we'd suggest to anyone adopting Pass^k as a gate:

I'd like to understand your closing point better. In our experiments, we didn't choose among individual guidelines: for each new task, we injected the guidelines derived from the most similar task. I'm curious where you see the disagreement about which guidelines to inject arising.

Fedora Linux 45 has been released. This includes all editions: Fedora Workstation, Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop, Fedora Server, Fedora Cloud, Fedora CoreOS, and Fedora IoT, as well as the Atomic Desktops and Spins.

This release adds support for installation on Stratis storage using Anaconda or Kickstart installs, retires unmaintained VPN plugins for NetworkManager, and updates Fedora's desktop environments, developer toolchains, and system packages. #9951. GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

The supply chain attack campaign's shift toward developer endpoints and cloud access signals what could be next for the cybercrime outfit.

A new wave of GhostAction attacks has largely failed, but this supply chain campaign operator is well-positioned to cause more chaos down the line.

GhostAction, an ongoing campaign in which attackers target GitHub by compromising developer accounts and injecting GitHub Actions workflow files into repositories.

Workflows tell GitHub Actions what code to execute when events occur (such as when a commit is pushed or a pull request is opened); these malicious workflows rely on GitHub's high trust in these files (by design), seizing repository secrets, package publishing tokens, GitHub personal access tokens, credentials embedded in source code, and much more.

The idea is that an initial compromise could be leveraged into more compromises and access points across repositories, CI/CD systems, and cloud environments, not unlike many supply chain worms observed in the wild lately, albeit functioning differently.

Related:Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

The campaign was first documented last year, and attackers continue to deploy GhostAction against organizations. What has changed is an apparent escalation of the technique beginning this month. During an earlier Oct. 8-12 wave, attackers pushed the security-audit.yml workflow into roughly 30,000 repositories, using compromised accounts to distribute credential-stealing code at scale. But GitGuardian on Oct. 27 published research highlighting further escalation. GitGuardian's Gaetan Ferry wrote that between Oct. 13 and 21, GhostAction's operator "pushed 72,000 commits to 23,000 public repositories," noting that 8,000 of them were new targets.

During this latest wave of the campaign, GitGuardian observed that once a developer account is compromised, the operator would deploy different payloads depending on which runner the repositories were hosted on. Runners are the systems that execute GitHub Actions workflows. Many organizations use GitHub-hosted runners, while others configure self-hosted runners that run inside their own environments.

These payloads include one called "seven workflows," which searches GitHub runner repositories and wikis for credentials including AI-provider API keys; the "Security-audit.yml" file seen in earlier GhostAction attacks that searches GitHub-hosted source code and Git history for credentials; self-hosted runner payloads targeting self-hosted CI runners; a payload targeting GitHub runners and AWS-requesting GitHub OIDC tokens (in order to assume AWS roles and achieve cloud account access); and the font stealer payload, which is the most notable workflow payload seen in recent attacks, due to its provenance.

Related:Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

The font stealer family installs a Node.js credential stealer on local developer machines, disguised as a VS Code task. The technique appears to be copied from PolinRider, a campaign that hides obfuscated loaders in developer repositories to steal credentials and has been associated with North Korea. The attacker also added PolinRider loaders between Oct. 22 and 26 to repositories already impacted by GhostAction. Ferry says that out of the five payloads, only the PolinRider-styled local stealer had a chance to successfully run, but GitGuardian has no evidence that any run actually occurred.

GitGuardian could not assess whether there was overlap between GhostAction and PolinRider, but hypothesized that GhostAction's operator possibly copied a public PolinRider launcher in order to target an overlapping set of victims.

Jenn Gile, cofounder of OpenSourceMalware (which previously covered the GhostAction attacks this month and detected signs of the PolinRider copycat a few weeks ago), tells Dark Reading that the PolinRider clone illustrates some of the inner workings of the GhostAction group.

"What we're seeing looks like imitation, not evolution. The fake-font technique in GhostAction is a copy of what DPRK's PolinRider campaign has been using nearly all of 2026," she says in an email. "The multiple payloads are real, but they're variations on a theme (five workflow versions over about ten days in one repo we examined), not a new capability. Historically, we might have called this evolution because it took real skill to figure out. But this looks a lot like an LLM helping the threat actor test different variants."

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

All of that said, GitHub identified and prevented execution of the malicious workflows, GitGuardian noted. However, importantly, the attackers still demonstrated persistent access to nearly 1,800 compromised accounts, many of which had already been used in earlier GhostAction activity; "1,382 of the 1,792 compromised accounts had already been used on Oct. 8, so the same stolen tokens keep working," according to Ferry.

Ferry tells Dark Reading that the campaign has been "highly ineffective on the malicious workflows side." But even if there's no sign this wave succeeded, the nature of the payloads (such as the one aimed at gaining cloud access) also shows where the attackers may intend to pivot next, toward internal networks where there are fewer platform-level protections that could thwart their efforts.

"We expect new waves to appear in the near future, with revised payloads," he explains. "This 'fail early and adapt fast' strategy has already been observed for this threat actor."

Given that targeted accounts or repositories remain compromised, repo owners should look for and delete the files that GitGuardian lists in the IoC section of the blog, on every branch. And, if signs of compromise are detected, users should revoke the account's tokens across the board and rotate every credential committed in the affected repository or its history, as well as every Actions secret and wiki credential.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Zero Trust Agent Systems that Pass Audits and Still Ship

Advait Patel shares a playbook for securing AI agent systems in production. He discusses moving defense boundaries from the prompt to the tool layer, enforcing scoped workload identities, and mitigating prompt injection via tool outputs. He explains how to structure audit-ready observability and implement kill switches to protect critical data while keeping deployment fast and compliant.

Advait Patel is a Senior Cloud Security & SRE focused on securing large-scale AWS and GCP platforms. His expertise spans Zero Trust architecture, vulnerability management, compliance controls for SOC 2/ISO environments, and distributed systems reliability. He is a Docker Captain, an IEEE Senior Member, and the creator of DockSec, an OWASP-adopted open-source container security project.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

When people talk about AI agents, they all think about some beautiful, nice, and fancy chatbots that can make their lives easier and all. Today, here, I need you to think about it differently. Today, I need you to think about that AI agents are not a new model, but those are a new identity. These AI agents are running in your environment, they're running in your system. Whatever controls or whatever security mechanism that you guys have built in your system, they are not applicable to this new identity. We need something to fight against this identity, because this is a fundamentally different aspect of your system. If you compare this new identity with other components in your system, they are completely different, because these new identities, they decide autonomously. They decide which API calls they need to make next, doesn't matter if it is your billing API, doesn't matter if it is your production database API, doesn't matter if it is your external email API.

If that agent thinks that it needs to do it to better easily answer the question, it will do so. This is how it is different first. Second is it holds state. Whatever that it ran in step one, it stores that context, it stores that information with it, and it still uses in step seven, doesn't matter if step one and step seven are different, but it still uses it if it thinks that it's helpful. The third is outruns review. By the time your engineer opens a ticket, by the time your engineer files and reports the issue, that agent will act faster, it will act in milliseconds, seconds, and then it will make 40 different API calls, it will call 40 different tools within a fraction of a second. This is before anyone can even recognize the issue or before anyone can even file the issue. That is why these are the new attackers. This is why this is a new identity where we don't have a security mechanism or we don't have any controls in place to handle or to fight against these identities.

Let me ask you about the AI security. When someone talks about AI security, people will refer to it as hallucination. I get it. Hallucinations are real, and that is a real question and real problem. Hallucinations are only limited, or that hallucination problem is up to the model layer, not the tool layer. Today, I need you to think about a different problem, which sits at the tool layer, and not the model layer, because that is where the blast radius lives. These four problems which I have listed here, are real problems that I saw and I faced in real production environments. The first problem is prompt injection via tool output. Up to this point, we were thinking that prompt injection via user input is the problem. For example, your user enters something malicious in your LLM algorithm or maybe chatbot, and then something happens, some bad activity or some malicious activity happens, and that is why you think that this happened because of the bad user query.

No, we are not seeing that in production environments, because we are all coming from a technical background, and we are all engineers. This is not happening in a production environment. Whatever your tool gives you, doesn't matter if it is a web page, doesn't matter if it is a document, or doesn't matter whatever instructions it is, they are malicious. Those retrieved documents is the real attacker here, because assume that those documents that tool retrieves, those documents that tool receives at the output phase, they can have anything, any malicious thing. You have a data breach. The second is privilege creep. Assume that your agent is now calling 10 different tools, and each tool has its own set of access and permissions, and now nobody in your team sat down and reviewed those permissions.

Nobody in your team sat down and think about whether this agent actually needs this many permissions or not, because all of those tools in combination gave that agent hundreds of permissions and hundreds of access, because no one was there to review it, and now it accumulated by composition. The third thing is unsafe retrieval. Context crosses tenant and sensitivity boundaries at retrieval time, because a query for one particular customer, the output and everything will be with the AI agents, and AI agents can now use that same output for other customers as well. With this situation, one customer data is crossing the boundaries and going to another customer data. This is the third problem, unsafe retrieval. The fourth is action amplification, like one ambiguous prompt that goes into the dozens of other side-effectful calls, because that agent thought that, ok, I will need these calls to make the answer better. These are the four failure modes that we are seeing in this production environment.

It doesn't matter if it is doing x number of steps, or it doesn't matter whatever it touches, but every session, every agent will get its own identity. For example, I use Workload Identity at work. The second layer is tools layer. This is very important. This is where most of the teams get it wrong. This is the important layer because your agents are using multiple tools, because in a production environment you cannot have one agent for one tool. It will be expensive. You have one agent using multiple tools, but each tool layer can have its own identity. It can have its own authorization, rate limit, I/O decisions. Doesn't matter what it is controlling, all the input, all the output. Also, it uses the short-lived tokens because we have to restrict the tokens usage as well. Each tool cannot have hours and hours of long operations tokens. If that work is done, then token can also get expired. We don't have to use the same token for other work. That's how we need to control it. When an auditor asks you, show me the token which was used for this call, then this is the layer that you should come and you should show the token. "This was the token that was used for this task. These are the operations that were made. These are the users who actually were attached to that token."

The third layer is context and retrieval layer. This is where you actually enforce the policy, because as a tool gave you the output in your document or web page format, this is where you actually enforce the ACLs per document. Basically, you cannot restrict what a user enters. You can have thousands of keywords, but those are not enough, because the LLM doesn't work in your favor when it comes to presenting the output. This is where you need to actually implement the ACLs, and you need to show, ok, these are the policies that I want this model or this agent to follow.

When an auditor asks you, show me the ACLs applied to the document retrieved here, then this is the answer to your question. As an agent, how that agent decided to pass this to the next step or how the agent decided to flag it and not pass it to another state. Those custom rules and everything will be applied here. Now if your auditor asks you, show me the policy version that was active during this incident, then this is your answer.

The last and important part of this architecture is audit and evidence. This is where you have the provability, this is where you have the actual evidence. Because these are the tradeoffs that I saw in an actual production environment. The first tradeoff was decisions in the hot path, because before you budget your tool, before you budget your AI agents and action, you also need to consider the latency as well, because one agent makes maybe tens or twenties of tools for that work. Each tool can take from 5 milliseconds to 20 milliseconds per call, so you also have to budget that when you sign or when you consider about SLAs. The second is token lifecycle. We talked about one token per work. We talked about one token per session. For example, if that call is lengthier than you expect, then token may or may not get expired within the work, and at that time, your AI agent workflow can be broken.

At that time, you need to think about, either I need to stop the agent, I need to kill the agent, or I need to let it run. This is the token lifecycle that usually is affected if there are lengthier tasks. The third tradeoff is fail-open versus fail-close, and that is where only you and your team can decide what sort of mechanism or thing that you need to put in fail-open versus fail-close. Thumb rule, which I follow, is I always put destructive operations in fail-close and read-only operations in fail-open, because if something bad happens, and if central policy agent gets broken, then I would rather stop my AI agent taking any destructive operations than stopping it from reading the tickets or reading the customer stories. This is where only you can decide what sort of operations that you want to allow in case of failure and what sort of operations that you want to just pass in case of failure.

The fourth point for tradeoff is cardinality, where per-session identity explodes label cardinality in traces and metrics, and this is something that usually surprised me most. The last one is policy as single point of failure. For example, you have one policy engine sits in the middle, sits in the central, and if it gets failed, then all of your AI agents will get messed up. They won't know which policy to implement and which policy to act upon. You need some sort of backup mechanism, where in case of failure of a central policy agent, you also have some backup where those AI agents can go and talk to.

Guardrails and identity and tools. Before we talk about guardrails, why do we need guardrails? Every AI agent needs some boundaries so that they can work within that boundary and also you have some control over it. The first guardrail which is very important is least privilege at the tool layer. What we do is we implement least privilege control at the prompt layer, but that is the wrong start. You cannot control user to enter the prompt. You can control the keywords that they can enter, but that is bad practice because it should happen at the tool layer because that is where the blast radius lives. The prompt can say anything. The prompt can do anything, but the tool layer is where you enforce what the agent is actually allowed to do. The second is scoped tokens only. We already talked about that each agent should only use token till that work is done, that per agent, per token, per session, per token.

Token should be scoped to current tasks only. LLMs should not ask nicely, can I please use this token because I need to do this and that? Can I please extend this token? That's not going to help. That's not going to work in the production environment. The third thing is tool output is untrusted input, because each tool will give you something in form of output. It can have malicious information. It can have malicious data, and that is where you need to control before it gets to the next stage. Those are the tradeoffs that we have seen in a production environment. Guardrails, these are the action, context, and kill switches. First is allowlist destructive actions, tier them by blast radius. You can reduce the blast radius. You can define what actions you want to put in each individual blast radius. You can have dry run. You can have explicit conform or human in the loop as well, depending on the tier.

The second is rate and budget limits per agent identity. Cost is security control as well. You need to also think about the sudden cost spikes when that agent is running. The third is bounded context. Hard caps on retrieval count, recency, and sensitivity class. Unbounded context is a data leakage surface for bounded context. Kill switch, this is another important aspect. You need to implement kill switch not after you are in incident, but before you even actually go and implement that AI agent, because you need some sort of control. If your logs or if your observability is saying that something is going south, something is not going as per the plan, or something is not going accordingly, then you need to stop that agent. You need to revoke that token immediately, rather than thinking about it later, rather than being an incident. This is something that you need to implement beforehand, not afterhand.

These are the failure modes. These are not the standards, these are not the regulations, but this is something that I came up with for our AI agents for our systems. These are the failure modes which are attached to the individual guardrails, and what compliance or what your auditor will require. Start with prompt injection via tool output. We talked about that prompt injection. It's not a model or it's not a prompt failure, but it's a tool's responsibility. You can implement output sanitization. You can implement tagged retrieval for your guardrail to handle this failure mode. Your auditor can ask you to give you the proof of validate and sanitize all the data coming back from external tools before the agent can act on it. The second failure mode is privilege creep that we talked about, least privilege model, where you need to scope the short-lived tokens per session, and auditors can ask you about each agent session gets only the permissions it needs and when those permissions expired.

The third is unsafe retrieval. You need ACL filter retrieval plus index and query time. For that, auditors can ask you to demonstrate that users and agents can only retrieve documents they are authorized to see and enforce at query time, such as action amplification. For that you can implement allowlist and blast radius tiering. Auditors can ask you about, define a list of permitted actions and evidence that high impact actions require explicit approval. Untraceable actions, so you need structured trace per call, identity link. For slow incident response, you need token revocation, and you need to implement kill switch. For those actions, auditors can ask you to show revoke agent access within minutes, and that you have tested this under realistic conditions as well. These are some of the failure modes that we have implemented. To overcome those failure modes, we have these guardrails that we have implemented. In our experience, these are the evidences that auditors have asked us to provide.

Have your eye on end-to-end components. Have your eye from starting part till end part with your logging. Shadow it for at least two weeks to get familiarized with the agent task and agent operation. Then, engage your SOC team before, not after, because they are the ones who are going to get paged first. They should be aware of your AI agent, rather than being an incident and getting, how come this agent came here? Once you see everything is working, then start implementing feature flag to control the agent and control the agent features and functionalities, to implement the kill path for the worst-case scenario.

The other question that I usually get from people is like, how can I convince my leadership team? These are the items like, it is a best practice, it is what's going in the industry right now: OWASP recommends it, other companies are also doing it, it's the right thing to do. Everything is fine, but these are the things that won't move the budget. These are the things that won't help you to convince your CFO, or convince your leadership team. Some of the things that I have seen work in my case or in most people I talk to. Talk about auditing cost. Talk about how you can reduce the auditing cost, auditing preparation cost with this sort of implementation, with this sort of AI agent, and how you have the observability in the end. Talk about the mean time to resolve for each incident. You can improve that MTTR by implementing this entire thing.

Your SOC team will also back you on this. Also, another important aspect is the cyber insurance. Cyber insurance risk committee now ask about agent controls explicitly, so this is one of the other angles that you can explore when you want to convince your leadership team. Also, another important one is, one incident pays for the entire investment. Just take one example, one incident from your past and try to implement something similar so that you can convince your team that, ok, we lost these many resources or we lost these many things because of this incident, and if we have something like this AI agent in production, we can save this. This would be your other argument.

For your Monday morning checklist or Monday morning takeaways, if you don't remember anything at all from this talk, just remember these three things. Move the boundary from the prompt layer to the tool layer, that is where your biggest and your blast radius lives, that is where your entire problem lives. Second takeaway is, treat every agent as a first-class citizen. Every agent gets its own identity. Every agent gets short-lived tokens not the long-lived tokens. Then the third takeaway is, build traces as audit evidence from day one, not after the incident or not during the incident because this is how you can have your eyes, this is how you can prove your compliance to other compliance people and your auditors as well. These are the seven questions you want to see if you are ready. Ask these seven questions to yourself, to your team. If the answer for all the questions is yes, then you are ready, if no, then you need to think about and you need to start implementing something.

For more information, I have been part of this OWASP CSA committees, and you guys can join the working groups, if you want to see what is going on and if you want to see how people and other teams are also doing and handling this situation, and handling this environment or architecture at different scale as well.

The question was more on blast radius and what are those blast radius and how we can identify. Blast radius, in technical terms, those radius are things that maybe your system can offer to lose something. For example, lower blast radius means if something goes wrong then it will only affect these components or these entities. Larger radius means it will affect the entire system, entire architecture, and so on. Only you or the developer or the architect of the system can define the blast radius. Then, for example, if this component or if this AI agent gets failed then how many components will get affected or how many entities will get affected. Those are the blast radius and that is how you can define them.

Participant 1: You said scoped identity, scoped credential, that's understood. What is the scoped token? Can you clarify more on that?

Advait Patel: Scoped tokens are for example, you are scoping any work for the agent, you are scoping or you are telling the agent that your scope is to not go and touch any production database. For example, if you want to get some idea or some familiarity you can have pre-production database, or you can go to dev environment, or you can go to verify environment to get that idea. Those are the scopes that you are defining, those are the scopes that you are telling your agent to follow rather than making those API calls, rather than going in the production environment and changing those environments or fetching those results. Those are the controls or those are the guardrails that you are telling your agent to follow. Those are the scoped tokens. For example, you can have your tokens per scope, you can have your tokens per individual, within the scope as well. For example, in your repo environment where you have multiple tenants or where you have multiple sub-environments, you can have your tokens per sub-environment or per tenant as well. That is how you can tell your agent to not go and do anything wrong.

Participant 2: My question is regarding the bounded context. In terms of the bounded context, I'm thinking of a couple of things. One is it's applied at the agent level or at the tool level, that's number one. Number two is, in terms of a user experience where I'm using the agents to answer the customers and all, if I'm applying all these rate limits, it might lead to a broken customer experience. Are there any strategies, where my customer experience could be smooth but at the same time I can block any malicious activity which the agent or tool might do.

Advait Patel: The first question was regarding the boundaries. The question was like, should we implement boundaries at the agent level or the tool layer? As long as you are not setting up boundaries at the model layer or prompt layer, you are fine. Because first is agent and then tools are underneath the agents. For example, you want more restrictive approach, you want more boundaries, more guardrails, then you can have per tool layer. I think one of the slides was saying that each tool has its own identity, its own authorization, its own authentication. It's better to have boundaries or better to have those guardrails set up at the tool layer because now your tool has all the set of permissions that it needs. Now you are going with the least amount of access or least amount of guardrails rather than providing everything to the agent. I think it should be at the tool layer, it would be better, but obviously not at the model or prompt layer.

#9949. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project showed they were worth trying.

Before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. New words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

The next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

The overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:

Will have to try it out. Data seems real good.

#9947. Shlemiel the Painter Is Back: How Zig’s libc Rewrite Made SQLite Slower

Back in 2001, Joel Spolsky â whose writings had a big influence my career â wrote a great piece titled Back to Basics. The premise of the piece is that practitioners should understand the basics: However abstract and remote we may seem from the basic algorithms that drive computing, they can unexpectedly have enormous consequences on our projects.

One of his examples is the âShlemiel the Painterâ trap, where a seemingly simple choice leads to quadratic runtime complexity. In that parable, a street line painter never moves his can of paint. As he gets further and further along in the line, increasingly more of his time is spent walking to and from his can of paint.

It is astonishing how often this Shlemiel the Painter pattern recurs1, including now in 2026.

A few days ago I posted about a chess analysis service I put online â2. This is primarily a Rust service backed by sqlite that dishes out analysis tasks to runners. Each runner processes upwards of hundreds of chess games and return a large set of JSON bundles back to the main service, where they are processed and then stuffed into sqlite.

While the analysis pegs two dozen cores on a runner for minutes on end, the process of storing the data should take milliseconds. Sub-milliseconds.

Imagine my surprise when on the first really large set of games, the simple process of inserting the JSON data â maybe about 40,000 records â into the data store took minutes. During all of my testing this never really appeared as a critical path, but with a large set of records it suddenly was a breaking problem.

What made this more perplexing was that it completely saturated a core, being a CPU-bound operation. How could inserting simple JSON into SQLite yield minutes of CPU time?

Shlemiel the painter has made an appearance. To drop a spoiler, he was introduced to the project via Zigâs cc compiler and its replacement for standard library functions.

The project isnât built in Zig, but instead uses Rust. The sqlx sqlite crate needs to be compiled for the target environment â sqlite is of course a C project â so to facilitate cross-platform building, generating both Mac ARM64 and Linux ARM64 / x86-64 binaries from this machine in a convenient build and deploy workflow, zig cc is used to compile sqlite when targeting Linux, generously offering up cross-platform targeting via cargo-zigbuild.

From one build and deploy script on my Mac I can target all of my platforms without containers or build machines. Zigâs elegant libzigc re-implements the standard library so you can static link the necessary functionality.

Zig uses musl (the standard library rewrite), but they have been rewriting it piece by piece in pure Zig (via libzigc), removing the C dependencies one at a time.

And thatâs where the performance issue was introduced.

In the rewrite of strspn, replacing the musl version with the pure zig variant), the first step measures the entire length of the string. This is also seen in the rewrites of strcspn, strpbrk and strstr.

This is a problem for tokenizers. A tokenizer takes a giant string and a common iterating step is to skip whitespace, getting the new string location and then repeating this pattern iteratively. With this shlemiel the painter pattern introduced with these rewrites, as it steps through the text it is tokenizing it is remeasuring the remaining length of the string endlessly.

This is what caused my performance issue, and itâs why it appeared on Linux but was never seen on my Mac (where zig wasnât used for compiling sqlite).

Tokenizing a 1.2MB file, which was seen passing json to sqlite, is approximately 12,000x slower with this pattern. As the file gets larger, the slowdown is quadratic.

I mean no malice or disrespect to anyone involved with these great tools that enable so much. But itâs interesting that in the year 2026, these same old issues can recur, and we all need to be vigilant for them. Something so trivial was grinding a process to a halt, in the most unexpectedly trivial of places.

My original fix for this issue, at least in my own code, was to pre-prune whitespace from JSON, which greatly reduced the cost when tokenizing in sqlite3, but not knowing where else it might bite I moved my Linux builds over to Linux containers.

Years and years ago, back when Sunspider was the go-to benchmark and browsers would herald their supremacy, the same pattern could be seen in the way Firefox handled string concatenations, causing it to be a laggard in that benchmark. Sunspiderâs benchmark run somehow entailed an enormous number of string concatenations â even the tests having little to do with strings â and a simple profile3 of a benchmark run showed that a significant amount of the runtime was consumed constantly allocating slightly larger string memory, copying to the new location, and then repeating this pattern. It was Shlemiel the Painter.

I corrected this (overallocate strings with a size-dependent buffer such that subsequent concatenations could reuse the buffer until it actually need to be resized again, which again would overallocate), blogged about it, Brendon Eich took note, and voila Firefox took the lead in the benchmark4. Such a trivial thing turned it from slowpoke to benchmark. â©

Iâm under no delusions Iâm going to support my family with a niche chess analysis service, and at most Iâm looking to break even with the costs of running it. I put it online because I found my work to these ends useful to my own game, and hope that occasionally it will find the right user without burdening me with the costs of doing so. â©

Profilers are awesome. They are the most powerful tool we have available to us, so itâs strange to me how seldom they are utilized. â©

And for what itâs worth, string concatenation was extremely common in almost all web projects, so the benefit was substantial in the real world as well. There was a best practice of using string builders, but so often people just slammed strings together in a loop. â©

Sharing what I built to get better at the game

#9945. Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Researchers can't quite explain why cyber threats look so different in Italy compared with everywhere else.

To read this article in Italian, click here!

Italy is suffering from a disproportionately large number of cyberattacks, new data suggests. Not only that: The kinds of attacks hitting organizations in the country are vastly different from those hitting other places. Researchers have a triad of theories as to why.

It's true that certain regions and countries face greater cyber-risk thanks to economic, military, and political factors. Israel is a magnet for hacktivists and regional, state-aligned advanced persistent threats (APTs). Brazil's unique history makes it a hive of banking Trojans. The United States economy will always draw the most attention from scammers. It isn't so obvious, though, why Italy is such a popular mark for cybercriminals.

"One of the main reasons why we decided to look into the Italian threat landscape is because Italy kept appearing at the top of our stats in our monthly internal reports," says Gianluca Tiepolo, cybercrime analyst at Intel471. In a report shared exclusively with Dark Reading ahead of its release, Intel471 found that Italy is a total outlier in the global cyber threat landscape. Organizations there are being compromised at a rate beyond what one would reasonably expect, based on the country's size, economy, and politics. And exploits against vulnerabilities and Web infrastructure are far more common in Italy than elsewhere.

Related:L’Italia è afflitta da vulnerabilità informatiche, senza una causa chiara

"We wanted to understand what was driving those stats," Tiepolo says. In the end, though, the data paints a nearly inexplicable picture of what's going on in the land of pasta and Chianti.

Italy is the 25th largest country in the world but, according to this new data, its organizations make up about 7% of all initial access data sold on cybercriminal forums. That's second only to the United States (30%) globally. Italy also ranks fourth among countries most targeted by ransomware.

Far stranger still are the types of cyber intrusions affecting organizations in Italy. According to the new data, initial access brokers (IABs) obtained their initial foothold through vulnerabilities in 57% of cases. Credentials only explained 23% of cases. Meanwhile, IABs have been selling access to victim-owned Web infrastructure in 49% of cases, with remote access and remote desktop tools making up 26% of cases.

So what? Maybe those figures don't pop off the page. Now, though, let's compare them with Intel471's own data from its 2026 Cyber Threat Trends & Outlook report:

Globally in 2025, IABs targeted remote access and remote desktop tools 67% of the time — 41% more often, relatively, than in Italy. Meanwhile, Web infrastructure — by far the most at-risk asset in Italy — represented such a small fraction of Intel471's global data that it didn't even bother to cite it in their report.

Related:Aussies Face Reduced Cybercrime Risk, as Pressure Shifts to SMBs

In the same vein, according to the company's global data, credential-based attacks are eight times more common in general than any other type of attack today. It found that 49% of IAB listings advertised credentials as the attack type, compared to 23% in the Italian-specific data. And guffaw-ingly, whereas in Italy they represent around 57% of all attacks, exploited vulnerabilities showed up in only 6.5% of cases globally.

Though cybersecurity data reporting can be interpreted in different ways depending on the circumstance, Italy does seem like a kind of cyber-risk unicorn, Tiepolo says, adding that Italy has been falling behind on cyber readiness for a long time now.

"I'm Italian," he says. "I've been working with a lot of different Italian clients. What I can say is that Italy is probably slightly behind other European countries, simply based on security technology [adoption]. For example, endpoint detection and response (EDR) technologies became popular in Italy around 2020–2021. Before 2020, most Italian companies didn't use EDR technology. So maybe historically, Italy is a bit behind in actually investing in cybersecurity products and technologies."

Related:Europe Evolves Into Ransomware's Favorite Region

Also, opportunistic cybercriminals are exploiting known, widespread, and often quite old vulnerabilities en masse to scoop up more victims in Italy than in other countries. "The data we saw last week from PHP2Shell, I think, validates this assessment. Italy is the country in Europe with the largest number of PHP 4, 5, and 7 versions, which are end-of-life," Tiepolo notes.

"A full 90% of initial access offers for Italy are what we call 'wholesale' offers," he posits. "They're not offers that are targeting Italy specifically, but simply exploiting vulnerabilities. Our assessment is that Italy is probably slower than other countries in patching their systems."

Another, related possibility is that Italy finds itself victim to a kind of cyber vulnerability network effect. The logic goes something like this: If certain technologies are especially common in a country like Italy, and organizations are slow to address vulnerabilities in those technologies, then that country becomes an attractive economy of scale.

As Intel471 wrote in its report, "Once an actor develops an effective exploitation method, the actor can apply that method to additional exposed systems without conducting a separate, extensive reconnaissance effort against each organization. This reduces the effort required to compromise businesses whose size or profile might otherwise offer limited incentive for a dedicated intrusion."

Researchers couldn't say exactly which technologies, vulnerabilities, or exploitations this theory might refer to, but noted that it does fold into the finding that 90% of initial access offerings to Italian organizations online are sold in bulk.

Without co-signing Intel471's data or conclusions specifically, representatives from the Milan-based cybersecurity firm Cleafy tell Dark Reading that they've observed broadly similar patterns.

"Our threat research does point to a related pattern: attackers reusing tools, infrastructure and techniques to scale campaigns across Italian banking targets," the company wrote via email. It pointed to cases such as the drIBAN Web injection kit, which attackers used to exploit the Certified Electronic Mail (PEC) system used widely across Italy. Cases like drIBAN "don't establish that Italy has a disproportionately large initial-access market, but they do illustrate how reusable attack techniques and infrastructure can help cybercriminals scale operations across multiple targets."

There is one other, potentially significant contributing factor to why Italy looks so different from other countries in cyberattack datasets: its prevalence of small businesses.

Most businesses everywhere are small, but, at least in comparison to other advanced economies, it's especially the case in Italy. A May 2024 "data snapshot for Italy" by McKinsey found that "MSMEs" — micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises — contributed roughly 10% more to Italy's economy and employment compared to their relative share in other advanced economies. And last March, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) published a report that cited that 99.9% of Italian firms in 2023 were SMEs, and 94.8% were micro-enterprises.

"Italy has a lot of small and medium-sized companies," Tiepolo says. "One of the things that came out from the data — especially the extortion data — is that these groups are [disproportionately] targeting small- and medium-sized businesses. So this could be one of the reasons [Italy stands out] in comparison to other countries that have more large companies."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9944. Jun Kim, oMLX creator and maintainer, joins Hugging Face to support the MLX community

We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are big MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

Stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

Our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for new ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

Concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make new transformers models run on MLX.

We are incredibly excited about the future.
