#9941. Shadowy AI Relay Disables OpenAI Codex, Claude Code Sandboxes

The enigmatic service is providing popular AI coding tools to mainland China and other regions where OpenAI and Anthropic products are not officially for sale — but with key security features turned off.

A mysterious relay service is installing authentic but unauthorized OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code tools for enterprise users overseas, and making dangerous configuration changes that put those organizations at risk.

The AI relay, first spotted by the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, appears to be designed to bypass regional restrictions that prevent certain countries and regions from using AI tools and platforms of US companies. According to Symantec's report published Thursday, the relay service installs genuine versions of the command-line interfaces (CLIs) for Codex and Claude Code on enterprise systems, but reconfigures them to route requests through the relay's infrastructure rather than OpenAI's or Anthropic's networks.

On the surface, this appears to be the case of a gray market provider or unauthorized reseller providing the AI tools to markets where they are not officially sold. Symantec researchers noted that the service, which has been active since early 2026, has installed the tools on systems at a dozen organizations, primarily in mainland China but also in South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia.

Related:Researchers Infiltrate Microsoft Tech Support Scam Operation

But the relay service also disables security safeguards for the tools, and the research team said it's unclear why it's being done (no malware or malicious activity has been observed thus far). One thing is for certain, according to Symantec: the relay service is creating enormous cyber-risk for the organizations using it.

Brigid O Gorman, senior intelligence analyst at the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, tells Dark Reading that researchers found a suspicious PowerShell downloader that they later determined to be "an AI-agent hijack script." After investigating further, the team found similar activity on other networks and traced it to the unauthorized relay service.

According to Symantec's report, when a user of the AI relay installs a legitimate Codex or Claude Code CLI through npm, the fileless PowerShell or bash script is fetched from "a lookalike domain by a one-line command that the user appears to run themselves. While this evokes the specter of attack techniques like ClickFix and InstallFix, the research team noted that the CLI clients aren't modified or Trojanized in any way.

And yet, the tools perform suspicious actions that heighten risks for enterprises. For example, the reconfigurations turn off the CLIs' execution sandbox, which is a key security feature because it limits what the AI coding tools can do.

Related:F-Secure Launches Victim-First Scam Encyclopedia Covering 50+ Types of Consumer Fraud

Additionally, the relay service enables network access for the write sandbox, turns off telemetry and error reporting features, and replaces the user's API credentials with relay-issued tokens. In one case observed by the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, the script logged a user out of their Anthropic session and deleted their authentication variables before reissuing credentials controlled by the relay service.

"Bypassing the regional restrictions that keep Western AI vendors from selling directly into certain markets is the simplest explanation, but it does not require disabling a CLI's sandbox or establishing persistent credentials that survive a reboot," the report stated.

The relay service activity is something of an enigma. The Symantec Threat Hunter Team said it's unclear why the operators of the client-side relay would need this level of control over users' systems, though the researchers did not observe any evidence of the operators abusing the access. The report noted that the architecture of the service would support malicious exploitation of the access if the operator's intentions were to change.

Furthermore, the Claude Code keys issued by the relay service are formatted with the prefix that Anthropic reserves for subscription-based OAuth tokens, "which is consistent with, though not proof of, a relay pooling flat-rate subscriptions and splitting the capacity across many customers," the team wrote.

Related:AI Slop Isn't Just for Social Media; It's Ruining Cyberattacks, Too

On the other hand, disabling security features hints at a potential fraud operation involving stolen credentials or payment cards, or even the malicious resale of prompts and files that run through the relay infrastructure. Gorman says it's "certainly notable" that the relay disables execution sandboxes and establishes its own persistent credentials.

"We did not see any malicious activity being carried out using these relay services, so any commentary on the potential intended goals of those using it are speculative," Gorman says. "However, a relay in this position can see every prompt, file, and secret an employee sends to the agent, and can alter or fabricate every response it returns. With the sandbox disabled and network access enabled, a malicious or compromised response could execute with the full privileges of the user's account."

Symantec provided indicators of compromise (IoCs) in the report, even though technically speaking there have been no compromises at this stage. "The organizations affected here look less like chosen targets and more like workplaces where individual employees found and used such a service to get access to tools they wanted," the report stated.

Nevertheless, the research team warned that using the service presents serious risk to corporate networks. And while the relay appears to be aimed at regions where Codex and Claude Code tools aren't officially offered, organizations looking for cheaper alternatives and users engaging in shadow AI activity could potentially find their way to such a service.

#9940. Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board

A four-question exercise that CISOs can use to create a threat model that promises results, without a big spend.

ISC2 Security Congress 2026 — Denver — A threat model should be a starting organizing principle for any security program. But rather than investing in a 200-page high-dollar threat model report, one longtime chief information security officer (CISO) argues that "four questions on a white board," can provide any team with an actionable plan forward.

Lora Vaughn, cybersecurity expert, former CISO, and now founder of her own consulting firm, The Vaughn Cyber Group, said that over her many years leading cybersecurity programs, she has developed a wickedly simple four-question threat modeling exercise that can be used in a wide range of organizations, be it the "National Security Agency (NSA) or your friendly neighborhood small-to-medium business (SMB)."

The answers, she said, can then offer a road map for investment decisions. That requires further exploration, she acknowledges, given there's always a new technology right around the corner that promises to drive down the cost of cybersecurity investment in enterprises. And reality must be balanced with industry hype.

Related:What We Missed: Knicks Phishing Test Goes Out of Bounds

For instance, around 2015, the move to the cloud was supposed to put the onus on providers like AWS to protect enterprises. What came next was a flood of misconfigurations and misunderstandings about who owned which part of security. By 2018, the buzzword was "automation." But teams quickly learned that automating anything required defining buttoned-downed processes first — often a prohibitively time-consuming exercise that pushed many of these project timelines out. By 2021, zero-trust networks were on everyone's mind. But that turned out to be less of a prescription and more of a customizable, guiding principle; and, architecting a true zero-trust environment requires a big investment in systems that would prove to be a much longer journey than many in the sector had hoped.

And regarding the current zeitgeist, handing over enterprise security to an agentic AI model is a "fantasy," according to Vaughn, speaking from the stage while presenting her four-question threat model at ISC2 Strategic Congress in Denver this week.

"AI is a force multiplier," Vaughn said. "It just multiplies what you already have. Zero times anything is still zero. Math is undefeated."

Bottom line: Once the threat modeling is done, choose your path wisely, and with your eyes wide open. And recognize that it's an ongoing cycle. "Refresh the threat model quarterly," Vaughn added. "Or after any big change."

Ask yourself, if you walked into work at 8 a.m. Monday morning, what would be the worst-case scenario(s)? For example, is it a ransomware attack that could result in the leak of sensitive information? What about one that locks up production systems? Mass pwning of firewalls and edge devices? What about a business email compromise (BEC) that results in a $100,000 bank transfer to attackers? Would falling for the North Korean fake worker scheme cause big problems?

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

Vaughn stressed that once identified, these should be ranked by pain to the business. She added, five to eight "painful" items are a reasonable number to determine.

Vaughn ranks risk in three categories: existential, painful, and annoying. Existential risk means that a breach would close the doors of the business. Painful risk equates to business disruption with associated costs and bad press. Annoying risk is something that can be fixed semi-easily.

A key piece of determining your risk profile is understanding who sees you as a target. Do state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) groups have your organization in their sights? Or is your business most likely to be targeted by BEC scams? Are ransomware affiliates trying to find a way into your systems? Do you have a large inventory of software or appliances that are high on attackers' hit lists? How is your patching hygiene, and do you have bugs that are known to be exploited?

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

This type of intel is free and available from sources like the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), but can also come from private threat intelligence services. Vaughn recommended that CISOs and security leaders lean on their vertical Information and Analysis Centers (ISACs) as well.

"That’s your most valuable resource," Vaughn said. "And it's free."

Items that fall between both the "worst-case scenario" and "who's targeting you" lists are where teams need to start first. "Every overlap is a scenario," Vaughn explained. "Write one sentence for each: who, how, against what, and costing what?"

In terms of a BEC attack, Vaughn pointed out a simple phone call verification could be the most effective prevention, and it costs nothing. "Find where the attack stops for the least money," Vaughn advised. "Spend in that order."

Additional free controls that actually work, according to Vaughn, are multifactor authentication (MFA) everywhere, which is something she adds is "non-negotiable" and urges CISOs to "fight for." An asset inventory is also invaluable, even if it's just a spreadsheet, and of course it "beats doing nothing." Patching bugs that have already been exploited, resisting the urge to give everyone admin credentials, and testing backups also make the list. And for ransomware, having backups isn't enough; network segmentation has to go along with it.

"If you can't restore from backups, or you don't have backups, you have hope," Vaughn said. "Hope is not a control."

She pointed out that nothing on this list of controls can be bought from a vendor. "There's no SKU for 'turn on MFA' and 'keep a spreadsheet,'" she added.

It might be tempting for cybersecurity teams to try and tackle these four questions on their own, but Vaughn said that including management in these conversations will help better align priorities to the broader business and will help management understand the potential fallout of not taking care of cybersecurity.

There are some best practices for doing this; for instance, Vaughn recommends linking spend to a business outcome: "If nobody funds a CVE, we stop shipping for a week," is one example she offered.

She also recommends bringing three spend options, with prices attached, and then making a recommendation for one. Additionally, Vaughn said CISOs and cyber teams should never promise "security," only reduced risk, and discuss investment decisions from that lens.

Offer, say, options that cost "$12K, $4K, or zero," she explained. "Zero means we accept the risk, so I recommend the $4K."

And once the decision is made, Vaughn suggested an email follow-up like, "Confirming we’re deferring X and accepting the risk of Y. Tell me if I got that wrong." That paper trail can prove invaluable following a compromise, she said.

#9939. [$] Portable Python scripts with dependencies

A basic Python script is portable: it can be copied between machines with little concern about compatibility. A script that depends on third-party packages requires quite a bit more care and consideration, however. In 2023, PEP 723 ("Inline script metadata") introduced a standard for declaring a Python script's dependencies inside the script itself. Several third-party tools can now automatically install and manage those dependencies, but there is still little official support for this standard within Python itself.

#9938. GNU Mes and the 0.28 release

From the series: GNU Mes interpreter speedup

It’s been a while since the latest blog post in the series but we have been working very hard behind the scenes 1. This means I’ll probably forget a few things from all we did, but there’s a good reason for that: we were making a release.

This is the first official and serious release I make as a (co-)maintainer, and the whole thing makes me uncomfortable. Even though people treat me as an expert programmer sometimes, there are many things in programming that I struggle a lot with. The first one, that I think I improved on in the last few years, is writing software from scratch. The second is delivering things to people.

This is normal, as all my career has been focused on R&D and that’s the way I’ve been trained to work. In the case of this specific release, something inside me still thinks my most valuable contribution was that: the idea and demonstration that this attempt could work.

Most of my career has been based on learning in a short time period the right amount of information so I can achieve a reasonable result. Then I normally move on to the next project.

Thinking about that, trying to read through my feelings, I started to realize more and more that whatever that drives me is pushing me to somewhere else, maybe to those parts I struggle more with…

Releasing code is important. It’s the only way to make people actually enjoy the result of your work. I have no problem to admit I struggle with this.

As an R&D guy I’ve always considered myself an “enabler”. I do something, I show how it is done and let people learn from it and actually implement it. That’s fine in some contexts but it has been driving me to some level of frustration recently, as the size of the projects I take part in grow.

An example of this is the RISC-V bootstrap on Guix. I spent a couple of years of my life working on it. We made a working bootstrap for live-bootstrap. But it’s not yet included in Guix because I delegated the final step. Now, even after the years I spent on that, all the sleepless nights and everything, it’s something I cannot enjoy fully2, and you cannot enjoy at all.

This “my job here is done” mentality is not enough for me anymore.

The kind of projects I do now deserve something else. I deserve better.

In Mes I had like 300 commits in a branch, pretty ugly, doing, undoing and redoing some stuff over and over again. The whole codebase was upside down, the commit messages were sometimes good and sometimes lacking, I had fixup commits that fixed things that were changed so much the amount of conflicts the reordering produced was overwhelming… It was a mess. It was me trying new things, learning and cleaning things up as I went. My arborescent thought process at its fullest.

In my usual way of doing things, I decided to promise NlNet a release, something I’ve never done before 3.

Once the bytecode adventure was done, showing some good performance improvement was possible and that Janneke made me a co-maintainer, it was the only acceptable thing to do.4

But, if I wanted to do it, I would need to slow down.

In the last part of the bytecode adventures, you remember how we included Popsyntax, and we reworked the whole macro expansion game. That wasn’t me, but Tim Sample.

I don’t remember very well how he joined my efforts here but I guess I bothered him with questions because he’s a long term Mes contributor and he’s also the author of Popsyntax, the Germ scheme implementation and many interesting things more.

He decided to start over. Chose a Mes release and walked through my steps. Removed the macro expander from the internals and wrote one in Scheme. From there, the direction was set.

I worked through the huge branch that I had, removing the stuff that turned out to be unnecessary, and he took over the git history, and made sure that every single commit was working.

I cannot imagine how many conflicts the guy has been resolving. But damn this looks good now.

This week, I released GNU Mes 0.28. The first release that I do as a GNU maintainer.

Janneke has been guiding me through the whole process — including the part of publishing the website to GNU using CVS5. I’m sure I would’ve never been able to figure out everything on my own. What a ride it has been!

But after more than a year of work, I’m very happy that most of the comments on the release have been positive, specially the ones from people that I worked with and I have a huge respect for.6

But, what will you find in GNU Mes 0.28 that we didn’t mention in the blog yet?

First of all, the main difference from the earlier blogpost is now Mes can be compiled with both M2-Planet and MesCC, and also with GCC as before.

It’s a tricky process, because the error reporting is very limited (I’m being benevolent here), and I was being a very nasty boy with some gotos inside switch statements. After some wrestling with allowed C syntax, I figured it out.

M2-Planet is limited, and we had to leave some things out. When Mes is compiled with M2-Planet it doesn’t have support for errors (aka exceptions) and those abort the interpreter, this is because M2-Planet’s C library doesn’t include setjmp. The stack operations had also to be rewritten as functions for M2-Planet, as the macros with array access were too complex for it. With that, Mes is a little bit slower when compiled with M2-Planet.

None of those are a big deal because that’s only the starting point of the bootstrap process and Mes is rebuilt with MesCC right after it.

The 0.28 release has been tested on real RISC-V hardware that I have access to,7 uncovering a few issues here and there in the Mes C Library.

First, the assembly parts that take care of program initialization in RISC-V (written by myself a few years ago, when I was working on the bootstrap) were broken.

setjmp and longjmp that we use for error handling in Mes, and were not used before, are also faulty. Because of this, the RISC-V version of Mes in the bootstrap, when built with MesCC that is, does not support errors until the issue is fixed.

I also found some extra stuff because GCC 14 decided that implicit function declaration warnings should become errors, breaking the bootstrap that we didn’t test in a very long time in RISC-V, first, because hardware unavailability and, second, because Qemu is also faulty for RISC-V.

There is still a known issue with M2-Planet-built Mes that explodes when it calls strcpy, this can be triggered running (procedure-disassemble map) in the REPL. We didn’t manage to fix this yet.

Tim reworked the macro expansion and made a simple and understandable initial macro expander in Scheme.

With that ready, many things started to fall off naturally.

Most of our driving issues simply disappeared. The macro expander takes the steering wheel from the start, giving us zero garbage collection issues during boot.

The earlier macro expander I wrote in C had to also drive execution, which could possibly call the garbage collector, killing all the C pointers that we had. The new macro expander does everything from Scheme, so no pointers are lost: gc_preserve and gc_release are gone. The boot-done! mark is gone, too.

As Tim started from scratch, all the API is way cleaner, and our initial driver is as simple as:

We can now use the stack for preservation, as it doesn’t happen that often, and the initial driver is a minimal loop that iterates through the few top-level expressions the initial boot file has (the macro expander). The rest of the program is run from Scheme.

Continuing with macro expansion, even if in previous posts we talked about Popsyntax integration, we decided to leave that out the release for now. We focused on having a faster interpreter with a new VM.

Keeping macro expansion simple, we are faster than ever.

These are the updated numbers from the 0.28 release comparing with the previous 0.27.2 bugfix release, released a week before.

This is running in my Tuxedo laptop from 2020:

You can see the times are similar to the nosyntax (it’s basically the same) branch we described in the previous post.

Take in account the numbers are tricky because mescc-mes means Mes building itself running MesCC. From one version to the other Mes changed, making it a little bit larger (+200 LoC), which means it should take longer to compile. The new version overcomes that, and even achieves a 40% reduction on execution time.

The fib benchmark is the most savage to me. There you can easily see how running has become way cheaper. On the other hand, mescc-hello shows how building a small hello-world program is more expensive, as Mes now needs to compile the whole MesCC to bytecode. When running MesCC for longer, like in a real program (mescc-mes), shows the startup time is compensated by far by the execution speed.

In summary, we got exactly what we were aiming for: a change so big the benchmarks don’t need to be precise. An improvement you can just feel by running Mes.

When I wrote the bytecode compiler I added a very annoying warning that complained about possibly unbound variables when you did something like:

This was later removed because the amount of warnings it was producing was really overwhelming and they didn’t really give us any useful information.

But! When I tested the bootstrapping process during development I realized they appeared twice. This led me to find the build scripts were compiling each file twice by accident.

So now, we are not just x2 faster in Mes. The bootstrapping is also x2 faster thanks to the annoying warnings!

Comparing to the code in the earlier post in the series, the released code has proper support for values and call-with-values that I thought I did right but I didn’t, really.

According to R7RS standard, the values procedure returns its arguments as values to the current continuation. If the continuation only accepts one value, only the first value is sent to the continuation. That’s what a regular continuation would do. With call-with-values the producer is called in a continuation that accepts multiple values that go directly to the consumer procedure.

If you take a look to the Guile case, that’s exactly how it works. Chibi takes the pragmatic approach not implementing the value discard and uses values just as a container. That’s what I implemented in the previous blogpost, but in the release I managed to do the standards compliant case, and make a REPL that now supports multiple return values, like Guile does:

The tricky part of values is solved with a very primitive support for continuation marks.

When call-with-values is called, the current frame is labeled with a mark, saying it accepts multiple values. When values is called, it checks the current mark in order to decide if it should keep or discard its arguments. It looks like this:

This whole thing works very well thanks to proper tail-calls, which reuse the frames so the marks are right in the current frame all the time. It’s clean and simple.

It also uses the simplest approach possible. The %values builtin wraps values in a list, adding an special car to it. core:cdr can be used to extract the list of values back from the wrapper.

Of course, we could do this “better” just putting the values raw in the stack, but this is good enough for now. If Chibi can get away with doing less, we should be fine with this.

I would never solve this issue if it wasn’t because some random research I did, encouraged by Tim and all the knowledge he has about Scheme implementations.

I was looking at a few papers on delimited continuations, like “Final Shift for Call/cc: Direct Implementation of Shift and Reset” by Martin Gasbichler and Michael Sperber, when Tim told me about his approach in Germ using continuation marks.

With that in mind, I made a very fast sketch on how would continuation marks look like and I realized that was more than enough for the values implementation I was struggling with when I saw the Mes tests (which I didn’t bother to run during the research time) started to fail for the value discard case.

I ended up using only the most minimal thing for it, but I hope to take it a little bit further in the future and make a proper continuation marks based Delimited Continuation support for Mes.

There are many things happening in this release. The diff is huge. But mostly you have been following the effort during the latest blogposts so there’s no need to go deeply in detail.

You saw me re-write the garbage collector, the macro expander, the driver, the builtin implementation, vectors and structs, values, continuations … Some of the code is gone (gc, macro expander and driver, the first implementation of continuations) but the knowledge stays. I basically visited every single corner in this interpreter.

I’m used to hop from one thing to the next. That’s the R&D me again. Now that I know this software the best, I don’t want to just go do anything else. Now I’m the best position to improve it further.

My goal for the future is to improve Mes in all those areas that I found it could be improved but I couldn’t focus on.

Delimited continuations are the best way to represent continuations in an stack based VM like the one I added to Mes. They are more lightweight, better for the GC, and they are composable, allowing for more sophisticated control. Guile supports them, so it would also help us get a step closer to Guile.

Pointer tagging could be a huge deal for speed and reduced memory usage in contrast to the tagged union approach Mes has. To give you an example, in a 64 bit machine each value is at least 24 bytes, including characters. This means if you (string->list "Hello") the result takes 24 bytes per cons cell, i.e per element, plus 24 bytes per character. Pointer tagging would put the bytes for the characters inside the pointers the cons cells have, reducing the total memory to just what the list needs (half of the previous case) and removing the need to access memory again to get the value of the characters.

With some type punning we could also revisit a few data structures we had some trouble with (mostly frames and templates) and make them flat and easy for the CPU to cache and access with no indirection.

In the case of the Scheme to bytecode compiler, just making it slightly better than the dumbest thing possible can make Scheme code fly: builtin inlining, avoiding boxing of non-mutated values… There are many things we can do while keeping complexity under control.

Some GC improvement is also needed, maybe with a simple generational-style garbage collector (does that exist?), at least for a few things like symbols and globals that are never collected it could improve the performance. Even if it doesn’t, we could always use some cleanup in the GC, which is very error prone now.

Those are low-hanging fruits that the new architecture made more accessible. If I just stop here they could be lost.

On the mid term, with all this together and all the improvements Janneke is doing, we could bring MesCC to the next level as a C99 compiler written in Guile that can be incidentally run in Mes.

On the long term, the GNU Mes project would become a very powerful bootstrapping toolchain for languages of any kind.

The GNU Mes development repository is now hosted in Codeberg, under the Mes organization8:

And we have opened an IRC channel at libera.chat: #mes

I tend to listen to my heart, my curiosity, gut feeling, or whatever you want to call it. That has pushed me to do uncomfortable things.

It is daunting, but it has been really rewarding.

The same way Free Software has made me learn how to program, GNU Mes has been an amazing training camp for the skills I was lacking: reading CS papers, preparing a release, writing code from scratch…

The project made me understand slowing down is sometimes the best way to go forward, and that I have to be more comfortable switching gears.

This is not just programming advice, but a general approach to life that I’m starting to understand as I get older —and hopefully wiser.9

Thankfully I’m surrounded by people I can learn from, and they bring the best version of me. All the crazy things that I attempt would have been impossible without the people I find in the process.

In this specific case of Mes, I’m very happy with the team we have. They supported me throughout the whole process, but specially during the release, when I was more insecure. I’m sure the next time I’ll be more comfortable slowing down and doing things right.

Thanks to them for the help, inspiration and support.

Thanks to NlNet and NGI for the trust and the chance to work in important but not-very-popular projects. Without funding, none of this is possible.

I hope we can continue to work all together for some time more.

We closed this one well. There’s no reason to stop here, though.

The “GNU Mes speedup effort” project has been funded through NGI Zero Core, a fund established by NLnet with financial support from the European Commission’s Next Generation Internet program.

I have mixed feelings with it, really. From time to time I come back to it and I cannot figure out how to do it. Then something else comes and I have to leave it. It’s a shame. ↩

Of something I’ve never did before (an optimization work) in something that I never worked before (a scheme interpreter). ↩

The other possibility was to chicken out, give Janneke the branch and disappear. ↩

Also, getting an email by RMS himself congratulating me for the release has made me a little bit emotional. Not gonna lie. I’m sure he does that for every release, but I’m a weak man. ↩

Thanks to my friend Iban for the SSH access. Siuuuh! ↩

My repository has been transferred to Mes. ↩

I can’t wait to hear people say this post is written by AI because of the em-dashes. I’m putting them here and there just to mess with them. ↩

#9937. Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

#9935. Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

An unreleased version of the AI model has found and chained multiple vulnerabilities in Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux, Anthropic says.

An unreleased version of Claude identified critical vulnerabilities in some of the world's most widely used browsers and operating systems and chained them into working exploits requiring little or no human interaction, Anthropic said this week.

The exploits included one that enabled data theft from a locked Android smartphone, another zero-click exploit allowed remote code execution (RCE) with root privileges on Linux servers, and a third that could have allowed attackers to remotely crash Windows systems. In total, Anthropic said, the model generated five working exploits targeting Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux. All affected vendors have addressed the vulnerabilities after Anthropic reported them.

The exploits are the latest evidence that frontier AI models are moving beyond simply identifying individual flaws to combining multiple into sophisticated working exploits. "These attack chains demonstrate the model's ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software," Anthropic's Frontier Red Team said in a blog post this week.

Related:Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

Historically, creating such chained exploits would have required special teams with domain expertise, the researchers wrote. "Now, it's something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify."

Anthropic's report described a one-click RCE exploit chain involving Chrome on macOS. The exploit combined four vulnerabilities in Chrome's JavaScript engine, memory protections, browser process isolation, and federated sign-in functionality.

Each of the vulnerabilities that Claude discovered helped overcome a different security control and allowed the chained exploit to escape the browser's sandbox. As a proof of concept, Anthropic's exploit launched macOS Calculator from Chrome when a user loaded a malicious webpage.

Anthropic said it reported 62 vulnerabilities to Google, all of which had been assigned CVE identifiers, rated high or critical, and patched by Chrome 156.

"For example, if the user is signed in to their email account, the attacker can now read their email; if they’re logged into their bank account, the attacker can view account balances or attempt transfers," Anthropic said. The exploit chain combined four weaknesses Claude identified in Safari — a use-after-free flaw in Safari's JavaScriptCore engine, a way to bypass WebKit's Gigacage memory protection, a vulnerability in the WebContent sandbox, and a JavaScriptCore flaw.

Related:Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

Apple has since fixed the issue, Anthropic said.

The Android exploit, meanwhile, targeted a locked Google Pixel 9. Claude chained three vulnerabilities in Android's device-transfer and USB-handling mechanisms, bypassing four layers of protection to extract photos and other personal information from the phone without unlocking it. Anthropic said Google has addressed the issue.

Claude's Windows exploit, which Microsoft has patched, involved a remotely exploitable denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerability. The flaw was an out-of-bounds read in the Windows kernel's implementation of the transport protocol used by HTTP/3. An attacker could send a small number of specially crafted network packets to a vulnerable server to crash it and repeatedly trigger crashes, disrupting access for users, Anthropic said.

For Linux, Claude developed a zero-click exploit against the kernel's networking stack that would have let an unauthenticated remote attacker execute commands with root-level privileges on affected servers, without requiring any user interaction. "This vulnerability (CVE-2026-98432) was patched upstream and backported to all maintained stable kernel branches," Anthropic said.

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

With AI getting better at discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities, defenders need powerful models for patching them before attackers can exploit the flaws, Anthropic said. "Enabling defenders with powerful models is critical to giving them a headstart on patching systems before attackers do," the company said.

To that end, the company is expanding access to its most capable AI models for vetted cybersecurity professionals through its Cyber Verification Program. The program now has three access tiers that give security teams a way to apply for the level of access appropriate for their work.

"It includes access to our most capable models, including Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Mythos 5.1, and other new models moving forward," Anthropic said. "Our advice to defenders remains the same: scanning your own code is more important than ever."

Andrew Bolster, senior R&D manager at Black Duck, says Anthropic's results are credible where they can be verified. The Chrome, WebKit, Windows, and Linux fixes are all public, he notes, but any claims that Claude discovered them autonomously are Anthropic's own. "The report gives no success rates, cost, or human-hours per chain, which is critical context for security leaders," he says.

Some of the conditions for the exploits to work were also noteworthy, he says. For instance, the Android chain involved a stolen phone and a USB cable, and the Linux exploit required an exposed MPTCP listener. "Exploit benchmarks show model success dropping sharply once ASLR, stack canaries, and sandboxing are enabled, and VulnCheck found only 1.3% of AI-discovered vulnerabilities confirmed exploited in the wild," Bolster says. "Delivery, reliability, and target preconditions remain the attacker’s problem for now, though I'd expect that gap to narrow."

Claude's chained exploits are another indication that AI has lowered the barrier to discovering vulnerabilities and building working attacks, says Jacob Krell, senior director, secure AI solutions and cybersecurity at Suzu Labs. But there are still substantial barriers between a proof of concept and a reliable attack in the wild. "A shell on one honeypot tells you little about the next server's worker count, build, or kernel," Krell notes. "AI has made finding the bug cheap. Getting it to work on a server it has never seen is still the expensive part."

At the same time, the gap between a proof of concept and a reliable, broadly deployable attack is increasingly becoming about time and target-specific adaptation rather than specialized expertise, he cautions.

Defenders are making a mistake if they assume this kind of vulnerability discovery always requires the most powerful AI models, adds John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security. "Local systems, including a Mac Studio with 128GB of memory or a DGX Spark, can support AI-assisted reverse engineering and vulnerability research. The target, model, tools, and operator's skill matter."

It may take attackers longer, with less capable systems, and attacks may be more practical only against smaller, less-scrutinized code bases. But defenders need to account for that capability, Strand says. "If AI can find vulnerabilities in Windows, Android, Linux, and Chrome, what does that say about code that receives a fraction of that attention? Think about your IP cameras. Think about the firmware on the router running a remote office. All of that is in play."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9933. How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

#9931. Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

As artificial intelligence squeezes early-career learning opportunities, capture-the-flag contests could be one way to help pick up the slack.

Artificial intelligence (AI) may be gobbling up entry-level jobs and learning opportunities for security practitioners, but it can't erase the value of hands-on experience with enterprise systems and security tools.

No matter how much agentic action cybersecurity teams embed into their security operations center (SOC) and the rest of their programs, smart people have to backstop that work. And the only way these "humans-in-the-loop" can do that capably is if they build up the kind of judgment that's best learned from the school of hard knocks.

The problem? With SOC tier 1 analysts becoming an endangered species and bug bounty programs on the ropes from a glut of AI submissions, the chances are dwindling for security newbies to rack up real-world experience.

There's no great fix to this career pipeline problem just yet, but some of the answers might be found in one of the industry's age-old mechanisms for both camaraderie and skill-building: the trusty capture-the-flag (CTF) competition.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

"CTFs give passionate talent the opportunity to grow and learn in ways that they might not have at their day jobs," says Jason Walker, a security engineer by day at software-as-a-service firm Five9. An avid CTF competitor, he won the Sentinels League competition sponsored and run by SentinelOne, beating two other finalists from a field of thousands of competitors worldwide. Besides street cred, Walker picked up a $5,000 prize for his efforts and a $10,000 donation in his name to his charity of choice, Trans Lifeline.

The livestreamed event offered up the spectacle and fun of an e-sports competition, but it may hold deeper clues as to how the industry can keep refreshing its talent pool in the coming years. As Walker puts it, CTFs are the ultimate way to expose both new and experienced cyber professionals to a wider range of problems and technologies.

"CTFs have helped me be a lot more versatile," he says. "If your company is running well and your program is mature, you aren't going to necessarily be firefighting new things every week. You're not going to be exposed to every new technique and threat. Doing CTF events and other hands-on training is a really important way to make sure you can stay up to date."

CTF competitions come in many shapes and sizes, but they fundamentally challenge players to find hidden pieces of data called "flags" buried inside intentionally vulnerable systems. Most fall into one of two formats: Jeopardy-style events, the kind Sentinels League runs, hand out standalone puzzles across categories such as Web exploitation, forensics, and cryptography, with points awarded per solve. Attack-defense events ask each team to defend its own vulnerable network while trying to break into everyone else's.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

The attack-defense format took shape at DEF CON's CTF, which started in 1996 and is still the event most associated with it. It has sprung forth a wellspring of CTF formats that range from grassroots industry events to big vendor-sponsored competitions like Sentinels League.

Sentinels League grew out of ThreatOps, a set of internal games SentinelOne's solutions engineers have run since 2020 to teach customers how to hunt through telemetry for hidden flags. This year's championship built on that with four games — Endpoint, Cloud, SIEM, and AI — spread across 12 weeks of qualifiers between June and October

The opening player pool of 2,236 entrants came from more than 100 countries, competing for a total prize pool of $100,000. Smaller prizes were dispensed across the qualifier and regional events, with the bigger prizes kept on reserve for the final, which was held in conjunction with SentinelOne's annual OneCon event.

Ryan O'Grady, director of SE operations at SentinelOne, says the firm invests the money in the prizes and the considerable logistics of running such a big event as a way to give back to the community, to build up expertise and exposure to its platform, and as a recruiting tool.

Related:AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

Whether motivated for the prizes or the training, the appetite for the event keeps growing. This year's drew enough interest that the company had to get a bigger ballroom to accommodate spectators.

Sentinels League is just one example of what a CTF looks like amid a much broader spectrum of competitions available. On CTFtime, the volunteer-run archive that tracks the hobbyist side of the scene, last year's calendar alone listed more than 200 individually organized events, with active teams from countries spanning every populated continent.

DEF CON CTF, often called the World Series of hacking, pulled 673 teams through its 2026 qualifiers before finals in Las Vegas this August. The National Cyber League, a nonprofit circuit O'Grady competes in, drew more than 7,500 students from 670 schools and universities this past spring. Kaspersky continues to run its own wildly popular SAS CTF out of Bali.

Other more academic events, such as New York University's CSAW and Carnegie Mellon's picoCTF, run versions aimed at students. Larger consulting firms, such as KPMG, use the format to scout corporate recruits.

In spite of the obvious demand for CTFs evident in the number of events held worldwide and the thousands of participants willing to sink their personal time into these pursuits, many security pundits worry about what AI is going to do to the purpose and purity of these competitions.

CTF organizers are thinking deeply about what this means for their rule books and how they enforce them. RITSEC's 2026 rules ban using AI to autonomously solve challenges outright, calling it against the spirit of the competition. Meantime, CSAW leaned into AI, this year creating an entire track built around using large language models (LLMs) to solve past CTF problems.

DEF CON CTF's 2026 qualifier split the difference. It barred fully autonomous AI teams but let human competitors use AI tools as long as a person stayed meaningfully in charge, requiring every team to label itself No AI, Low AI, or Human-Led AI on the public scoreboard.

A recent study of hundreds of Hack The Box machines released between 2017 and 2025 found solve times dropped roughly 16% a year, with the steepest declines after 2022. The hardest tier of challenges went from a 15-hour median solve down to about five, according to penetration tester Jacob Krell of Suzu Labs, who did the analysis.

He's not the only one worried. An academic study earlier this year from IBM Research and the College of William & Mary pitted 41 participants in a live, on-site CTF against four autonomous AI agents. It found that those agents placed second overall, ahead of most of the human teams competing.

Findings like these are enough to get firms like OtterSec, a blockchain security firm, to make noise about how to "save" CTFs. This summer the firm launched a $100,000 "Save CTFs Fund" to bankroll new formats that stay meaningful as AI keeps improving.

SentinelOne's O'Grady doesn't buy the death-of-CTFs talk. In his view, AI just forces organizers to redesign CTFs so they still force a human to think laterally, AI assistance or not.

AI may not be killing creative CTFs anytime soon, but it is definitely making cybersecurity's career ladder wobble. In the process it may actually be making CTFs even more crucial.

SANS Institute polled nearly 1,000 security leaders and found unclear career progression to be one of the top hiring challenges, cited by 32%, more than triple the rate last year. Only one-quarter of organizations say they have a clearly defined career path, and entry-level jobs that used to train the next generation of defenders are diminishing. SOC and security analyst roles lead the AI-driven cuts, down 32%. Threat intelligence analysts are next, at 26%, with incident responders close behind, at 22%.

Bug bounty programs are buckling under AI's pressure. At the start of the year, maintainers of the open source project Curl shut down their program after a massive influx of junk AI submissions. HackerOne paused its Internet Bug Bounty program in April after a wave of low-quality, AI-assisted reports flooded in. And this month Google Bug Hunters also paused its open source bounty program due to similar problems.

These are all blows for cyber career progression, as bug bounty problems were another great place for security professionals to flex their skills publicly and for newcomers to gain a foothold into the industry.

As long as CTF organizers can keep their competitions relevant, these events will remain a valuable puzzle piece in the skills training picture for the industry, alongside other important hands-on challenges like cyber ranges.

"With LLMs basically sweeping the table on bug bounties, it's become even harder than it already was for people to get out there, show off their skills, and get their name out there," O'Grady says. "AI has only increased the importance of CTF events like this."

An award-winning freelance reporter with nearly two decades of experience covering B2B cybersecurity, Ericka Chickowski has tackled every angle of security and risk for Dark Reading since 2009. Her coverage has spanned the full range of cyber topics important to every kind of cybersecurity stakeholder, including cybersecurity practitioners, CISOs, security-minded business managers, and security-aware board directors. She specializes in going deep on topics, breaking down how the technology trends affect real people, and how risk impacts the bottom line.

Some special areas of focus include: adversarial AI; AI risk and resilience; AI and agentic governance; application security (AppSec); governance, risk, and compliance (GRC); cloud security; network security; software supply chain risk; cyberinsurance; DevSecOps; enterprise risk management; and CISO career development.

In addition to Dark Reading, Ericka has written for many different IT and business publications over the years. Her byline has appeared in dozens of trade and consumer magazines, including Baseline, Consumer Digest, Channel Insider, CIO Insight, CSOOnline.com, DevOps.com, eWeek, Entrepreneur, Forbes, InformationWeek, SC Magazine, and SecurityBoulevard. She regularly contributes independent stories about AppSec and supply chain risk to the ReversingLabs Blog. She was one of the founding contributing editors for DevOps.com and has deep expertise in digital transformation and development best practices. This helps inform her stories on software risks and business resilience.

Ericka is also a prolific executive ghost writer, with experience helping cybersecurity and IT leaders bring their ideas to life. She's helped them craft important position pieces for respected publications like the Financial Times and The Wall Street Journal.

Prior to beginning her freelance career, Ericka served in a number of editorial staff roles, including West Coast Bureau Chief for SC Magazine. Before that position, she was editor-in-chief for a cluster of regional technology and lifestyle magazines in the Seattle area, as well as a beat reporter for a regional business newspaper. #9930. Welcome RL Environments to the hub

Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it."

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

#9929. Critical security vulnerability affects OpenSSH on Alpine Linux systems

Version 10.6p2 of OpenSSH has been released with a workaround for a critical vulnerability that affects Linux systems that use musl libc with PAM disabled, such as Alpine Linux. OpenSSH developer Damien Miller said:

If you operate a Linux system that uses musl libc without PAM (Alpine Linux is one example) then stop reading and set PasswordAuthentication=no or disable SSH for these systems IMMEDIATELY.

This vulnerability does not exist on non-Linux systems, Linux/glibc systems and Linux systems that use PAM for password authentication.

We consider the root cause of this bug to be outside OpenSSH itself, but we're in a good position to deliver a mitigation quickly.

The Alpine Linux project has announced that it will be backporting the OpenSSH fix "all the way back to Alpine 3.16", which was released in May 2022.
