#9928. Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

This installment of the Reporters' Notebook video series discusses some of the trends and topics from Cybersecurity Awareness Month, from using AI for better training to educating next-generation workforces on modern risks and emerging threats.

AI is changing the concept of cybersecurity awareness in more ways than one.

In the latest installment of our monthly Reporters' Notebook video series, Cybersecurity Dive's Eric Geller, TechTarget Cybersecurity's Sharon Shea, and Dark Reading's Rob Wright discuss some of the trends they've observed during Cybersecurity Awareness Month, which has shifted during the AI era with the emergence of news threats as well as revamped defense strategies.

As we’ve seen in years past, cybersecurity awareness training often becomes a compliance checkbox exercise rather than a vehicle to educate employees and users on the latest threats. And unfortunately, the threat landscape today is changing at a frenetic pace. Threat actors are taking advantage of AI tools and platforms to accelerate, enhance, and scale their attacks, whether it's social engineering schemes or wide-ranging supply chain compromises.

Thankfully, as the editors explain, some organizations are updating their programs to take more specific, line-of-business approaches for training while also accounting for the evolving threats related to AI; some programs are even using AI to create more convincing phishing simulations. Meanwhile, several US colleges and universities have increased their education offerings for AI security.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

The editors discuss these topics and more in this Reporters' Notebook episode.

Learn more in the video, and also check out other Reporters' Notebook episodes, available here, for insights and coverage from across Informa TechTarget's network of cybersecurity sister sites.

This transcript has been edited for clarity, readability, and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant and human editors. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Rob Wright: Hi, I'm Rob Wright, senior news director at Dark Reading, and welcome to another edition of the Reporter's Notebook. I am here with Sharon and Eric. Would you guys like to introduce yourselves and then we'll get into the topics for today?

TechTarget Cybersecurity's Sharon Shea: Hey, I am Sharon Shea. I'm the lead editor on Tech Target Cybersecurity.

Cybersecurity Dive's Eric Geller: And I'm Eric Geller. I'm a senior reporter at Cybersecurity Dive.

DR's Rob Wright: And this month is Cybersecurity Awareness Month. Yay! I know it's our favorite time of the year, right? We've written a fair amount of content on this topic over the last few weeks. We're still in it. We've still got about a week to go. It's not been a great run recently. There's been a lot going on, a lot of attacks, a lot of threats, a lot of urgent stuff going on in cybersecurity. But we wanted to get into some of those things here in this video discussion. Sharon, do you want to kick us off?

Related:Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It

TTC's Sharon Shea: Yeah, so I will kind of take it back to the human side of Cybersecurity Awareness Month and then we can jump into some of the attack stuff later. But you know, one of the big things in Cybersecurity Awareness Month is making sure that your training programs are up to par. And granted, it's not just this month, just like Earth Day is not just one day for the Earth. We want it to be year-round.

But it does kind of give a springboard, as we called it in one of our articles, to further focus on cybersecurity throughout the year and bring a renewed focus for this month. And one report I was reading, a SANS report, said that 19% of organizations have cybersecurity awareness training programs designed primarily to meet a specific compliance or audit requirement. And that's kind of a bad way to look at things, just doing this for compliance.

Obviously, you want to do it to be secure all the time. And, you know, we all probably groan when those awareness trainings come into our inboxes every couple months or a couple times a year. They can be boring and you just click through them just to get through them and do the checkbox. But sometimes those aren't quite as effective as they should be, as we've seen. Really, you don't want to treat it as a check space, compliance checkbox exercise.

Related:As AI Risks Grow, Insurers Split on Covering the Damage

And one major thing that we learned from our reporting, or I think we've known for years, but it's not one size fits all, right? You really want to identify the behaviors within your organization that create risk. You want to map those threats to business consequences, establish baselines, and monitor for deviations from those.

Threat s like deepfakes trying to get into your help desk and reset MFA or, you know, the common Arup example of the CFO who was on a call with an employee and wanted them to wire a ton of money to them. And you know, you really have to focus those down on what departments really need specific trainings. I guess within the organization, you have so many different types of people to cover. You have your general employees, you have C-level, privileged admins, HR recruiting, customer-facing employees, and you have third parties, contractors, and you want to match the awareness to those sorts of risks.

I guess another thing that we can talk about too is updating the program regularly. You do want to talk about older tech. We all know that phishing is a major thing, right? It's still a problem, but you also want to talk about the newer tech — AI. And not just AI — GenAI, agentic AI, you know, all these newest technologies from the past couple of years. People know how to securely use them as well as preventing their inherent security issues.

And another thing I thought was kind of cool that we've covered is using AI in your awareness programs. We were talking to one CISO who uses phishing — I'm sorry, uses phishing simulations created by AI to personalize them for their employees, which you know is pretty cool, too. It's not just that generic boring watching the same old video from, you know, the 1900s, probably.

TTC's Sharon Shea: Yeah. You know, so kind of to solve some of the problems too of those boring programs. One of our sources, Kevin Walker of Black Swan, told Alissa Irei that you know, you really want to do short training sprints versus real world marathons. Those hour-long trainings, no one's going to get them. You know, they're not gonna pay attention throughout this whole thing. So make them highly relevant, personalized, and you really want to have those short, easy-to-consume bits that are good for your employees.

I guess talking about specific threats towards specific employees, Rob, you had an example that you guys have been covering on Dark Reading lately.

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah, there's a lot going on lately with AI-themed attacks. And one of the things I've noticed — we covered this a couple, a few times actually — is that there's a lot of SEO poisoning and malvertising. I think we think of like malvertising and threats like that as kind of like low-hanging fruit, kind of the type of attacks that aren't very sophisticated and that don't go very far. Maybe you get like some malware on your system from a flash ad or like a comb-over ad or something like that.

And we're finding that these ads are getting a lot more — I hate using the word sophisticated, I hate it so much, it's so overused — they're getting more effective. There's not a lot of ad blockers that are going to get you around ads on Facebook and Meta, for example. And there was a recent report from Gen Digital — well, I think it was almost a year now — that they found that one out of every three ads on Instagram and Facebook was malicious. It either pointed to malware or some type of phishing link, or it was a scam, like an outright scam.

And what's happening these days is that attackers know that they can use sponsored links and they can use these types of ads, not just your conventional like pop-up ads and stuff like that, which a lot of people do block. But they can use those sponsored links, you can use Google ads, you can use really effective SEO poisoning techniques to put stuff out like, 'Hey, download Claude Code' or something like that, or like a new AI tool.

And there are so many people out there looking for these tools right now. There are so many people, there's so much shadow AI that it's just easy to come across one of these malicious links, whether you're actively looking for it or you're just playing around — who knows? And they're hosted on legitimate infrastructure, they're hosted on — there was a report recently that Any.Run had, there were some stats about how many attacks, AI-themed attacks, are being deployed and there was a report about just massive use of Cloudflare Pages as infrastructure so it looks legitimate and then there's also like OpenAI Custom GPTs and that like that just it just looks legitimate because it's on like a real provider like it's on OpenAI or it's on Cloudflare.

And it's very easy to get tripped up by these things and click on something and then immediately download an infostealer that gets your credentials. And if you're a developer, there's been so many attacks on developers. And it's just bad news for an organization. So I think one of the things that companies ought to focus on right now is just trying to get people within the organization — obviously it depends on like what your privilege level is and where you are in the organization — but really for any type of employee that's out there looking for an AI tool, you've got to know the risk. You have to know that a lot of the stuff that you're going to be digging up out there, if it's not through an official app store of for an official channel, it very well likely could be a scam or some type of social engineering scheme that's going to drop an infostealer or something worse on your system. So that was kind of an eye opener for us.

Scary stuff. And we're not even to Halloween, so we'll see. Eric, what have you been seeing?

CD's Eric Geller: Well, I looked at things from the perspective of the next generation workforce. We're talking a lot about educating the workforces of today and trying to mitigate the threats of today. But we're also seeing a lot of change in the AI landscape that it's been difficult for the current workforce to get their heads around. So I kind of focused on preparing the next workforce to understand not only AI, but also how to guard against threats related to AI.

So, how to be an AI security practitioner, how to focus on AI security governance and risk management. And I looked at the university level to understand what kinds of courses exist out there to prepare students for careers in this area. It's no surprise that there's a lot of AI curriculum at the higher education level. What might be more of a surprise is that universities have actually gotten pretty good over the past few years at recognizing that there needs to be a security component to that work.

So I spoke to people at a number of schools that have tried to build or begin building curricula around AI security. Spoke to folks at Carnegie Mellon. They have a certificate program in AI security that's designed for kind of mid-level corporate workers who want to specialize in this area to go in for a class. It's a few weeks, you come out with a certificate that can kind of prepare you to be a leader in this space. But of course, a lot of this is happening at the undergraduate and graduate level. And so there's a lot of courses designed to kind of grab folks at that point in their early, early pre-careers, if you will, and teach them why this is an important subject.

So I spoke to a professor at Georgia Tech who is teaching a graduate course in LLM security and said that she was actually surprised by how much interest there's been in AI security when she teaches you know, undergraduate level sort of cyber one one and she talks about large language models, there's a lot of interest in following up outside of class and trying to learn more about that specific part of cyber.

For those of us who are perhaps a little pessimistic that college students want to focus on security when all the money and the attention is in building and deploying new products, I think this story that I wrote was kind of a somewhat of a corrective to that narrative, but also just as a source of optimism that at least according to the folks who are teaching this material, there are folks interested in learning about this kind of stuff and there are folks interested in pursuing graduate school education and getting certificates specifically in the security part of AI, which again is good to see. And I think we're going to start to see a shift over the next few years as people come out of these programs and begin entering the workforce. We're going to see a more security minded attitude, I think, toward AI development, at least if some of these colleges get their way.

DR's Rob Wright: I'm actually, I suddenly have a positive outlook, which is really rare for me. I'm normally the pessimist.

DR's Rob Wright: Thank you. Yeah, no, that's great news. it sounds like a welcome development. So maybe there is something to look forward to with AI. Fingers crossed.

CD's Eric Geller: Yeah. And the one thing I'll add is that this is not just something that's siloed at specific universities. There are coalitions of schools working together to create curriculums, curricula that that they can you know use interchangeably, taking best practices that one school has found in terms of what works for teaching in the classroom, sharing that with other schools.

This is one area where the federal government is actually kind of playing a behind the scenes role because they sponsor this nationwide coalition that has sort of different schools have taken the lead on building their own little groups of schools that they work with to kind of create lesson plans, find subject matter that works in the classroom, and then share those lessons with each other. You know, academia is obviously a very collaborative sphere, and I think that works out to everyone's benefit here because the teachers that are finding things that work are are telling other teachers and other professors in other schools, you might want to try this approach. And there's a consortium that is kind of bringing all that together and trying to make this not necessarily the exact same curriculum at every school, but shared curricula across universities.

DR's Rob Wright: That's good. I'm optimistic, and I'm never optimistic. Well, thank you guys for coming together to discuss Cybersecurity Awareness Month and I'm glad we're ending it on a positive note. Thanks guys.

TTC's Sharon Shea: Thanks, Rob. Thanks, Eric.

InfoQ Homepage News Building a Culture for a Kubernetes-Based Platform in a Bank

Nov 05, 2026 3 min read

In a banking environment, open source can earn trust by running real workloads, as Marcy Paramonova and Stéphane Cusin explained in their talk Building Cloud Native Culture in a Bank at KubeCon & CloudNativeCon Europe. Deploying Kubernetes was the easy part; the hard part was culture: community of practice, shared knowledge, rituals, ownership. Teams try things, keep what works, and improve bottom-up.

Open source was not an obvious choice in their banking environment, Cusin mentioned. They received questions about support and accountability. Instead of trying to convince people with theory, they started running real workloads. Over time, trust was built by operating the platform day after day:

Open source stopped being seen as a risk. It became the foundation.

They treated their first version of Kubernetes like a project. "We delivered it, we got a good adoption", Cusin said. But the operation was incredibly hard. Not because the technology was broken, but because they hadn’t built the culture around it yet:

Nobody knew who to call, responsibilities were blurry, and teams were consuming the platform without really contributing to it. Every incident felt like a fire drill.

They realized deploying Kubernetes was the easy part. The hard part was building the culture with a community of practice around it. The shared knowledge, the rituals, the ownership model, Cusin explained:

Without that culture, no platform survives its own success.

They invite people to experiment, for instance by having a yearly competition where everybody can submit their ideas and the one that wins, actually gets implemented. Many of their improvements came from the bottom up, Paramonova argued.

They used open source as a compass, something that helped them orientate a subject, Cusin explained:

When Kubernetes appeared, we recognized it immediately. Strong Kubernetes, transparent governance, and real production users. The compass pointed; we followed. And now we are watching OpenStack the same way.

A compass doesn’t force you in one direction. It helps you recognize the right opportunity when it arrives, Cusin said.

They tried things, and some of them didn’t work. They kept the ones that did. The act of trying, of deliberately designing how teams interact, creates the culture we have today, Cusin said. Structure first, the culture follows.

Every organization is different; every regulated environment has its own constraints, Paramonova said. You need a compass during your journey. It’s something that will guide you when everything else is uncertain. For us, it was open source, she concluded.

InfoQ interviewed Marcy Paramonova and Stéphane Cusin after their talk.

InfoQ: How did you gain trust from your development teams?

Stéphane Cusin: Over time, trust emerged from a combination of transparency and reliability. When developers see that the platform consistently helps them deliver applications safely and efficiently, adoption follows naturally.

Marcy Paramonova: Trust was not something we could establish by presenting a roadmap or writing good documentation, though both matter. It came from running things. From being present when something broke. From being honest about what was not yet ready.

Cusin: Today, our culture is centered around ownership, automation, transparency, and continuous improvement. Teams are empowered to move quickly, but they do so within a framework of shared standards and platform capabilities. The result is not only greater efficiency, but also greater consistency, reliability, and visibility across the organization.

InfoQ: How did Kubernetes transform how your organization builds software?

Cusin: Kubernetes gave us a common platform and a common operating model. In the first version of our platform, we gave teams flexibility. We exposed many Kubernetes capabilities directly and allowed teams to customize their deployment model extensively. In practice, that often resulted in different patterns emerging across teams.

One of the lessons we learned as platform engineers is that developers do not come to a platform looking for more infrastructure choices. They come to a platform to deliver software.

In our current platform, Kubernetes is no longer the product. Kubernetes is the implementation detail. The product is a simple, secure, and standardized software delivery experience.

We provide opinionated deployment patterns, standardized Helm charts, and common platform capabilities. As a result, when an engineer moves from one team to another, the deployment experience is largely the same. They do not need to relearn how applications are packaged, deployed, monitored, or operated.

Paramonova: The transformation I experienced most directly was organizational. Kubernetes gave teams a common language. It created shared abstractions that made collaboration across different parts of engineering much more natural.

Before, a lot of knowledge was siloed by team or by technology stack. Kubernetes did not erase those silos overnight, but it gave everyone a shared foundation to build on. That changed conversations, and changed what was possible.

#9925. Holo4: powering generalist computer-use agents

Holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

AutomationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

The tower is square in plan at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

Four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Build a 3D model in FreeCAD of the H company logo: a solid filled disc beside a blocky sans-serif capital letter H, both extruded to the same thickness, the two shapes of similar height and set apart so they do not overlap, with the centre of the disc level with the middle of the H. Colour both shapes black.

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

No one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines)

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines)

Our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

These gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

#9924. A Look at Datastar

I have always been interested in frontend solutions for building web applications. Even though I’m more of a backend programmer, I really dig all the different techniques people come up with for creating browser-based apps that are both reactive (reflecting remote state in real-time) and interactive (responding to user actions).

Over the last few years, I’ve been looking at different frontend frameworks and libraries, to see how they work, and what I can learn from them. I adore Svelte, which is really smart and efficient. Its sister framework SvelteKit inspired the file-based routing in my own web framework for Ruby, Syntropy. I also really like the approach of the Phoenix framework to building reactive apps using LiveView, which is an amazing technology that builds on the solid concurrency foundation of Elixir/Erlang.

Many people have tried to recreate the same functionality for other languages or frameworks, with varying degrees of success. Recently, Marco Roth came up with ReActionView, which promises to bring reactive views to Rails apps, building on his previous work on Herb, a set of tools that improve on the developer experience of writing ERB templates for Rails apps.

All those different technologies are certainly impressive, but they all are tied to specific languages/frameworks: Svelte/SvelteKit is a JS framework, LiveView is for Phoenix/Elixir, ReActionView is for Ruby on Rails, LiveWire is for Laravel/PHP, etc.

And then there’s Datastar, which dubs itself “the Hypermedia framework”. It is somewhat similar to other frontend declarative frameworks/libraries such as HTMX or Alpine.js, in that interactivity/reactivity is done declaratively by adding attributes to HTML tags. But what is different about Datastar is that it insists on keeping state where it should be, such that it doesn’t try to copy server state to the client and keep it in sync with the server. Instead, the server continuously sends updates (in the form of HTML patches, or signal patches) to the client. In that respect, Datastar is more like LiveView, but without the coupling to Phoenix/Elixir. In fact, Datastar offers SDKs for different languages and frameworks, including Ruby (the Ruby SDK is maintained by Ismael Celis).

I find this approach so refereshing! With Datastar, you can use any backend technology in order to build reactive web apps. Furthermore, Datastar relies on SSE (server-sent events) for streaming updates from the server to the client, instead of the somewhat older approach of using a WebSocket connection used in technologies such as LiveView, or HotWire (the current go-to solution for Rails apps).

While SSE does not provide a full-duplex connection to the server (meaning, you can’t use an SSE request/connection to send data from the client to the server), it provides two important advantages over WebSocket: A WebSocket connection normally requires establishing a separate HTTP/1.1 connection to the server (there’s partial support for WebSocket over HTTP/2, but that depends on the browser and the server/reverse proxy used. HTTP/3 support is very limited as far as I could tell). In contrast, SSE requests can be multiplexed on top of an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection, along with any number of other concurrent requests. Secondly, because SSE requests are just normal (streaming) HTTP requests, the server can use standard HTTP compression in order to achieve significant reduction in bandwidth.

Let’s look at a simple example of working with Datastar. Here’s the markup for a simple reactive app that displays the current time on the server:

This example does three things: load the datastar library (BTW it’s only about 15KB!), set up a connection to an SSE stream at /ds/time_stream using the @get action, and binds a span to a signal named $time. On the server side, the controller looks as follows (using Syntropy):

The controller code is quite simple: after calling respond_sse, which sends some HTTP response headers, we send a first update, then we send further updates once per second. What actually gets sent over the wire looks as follows:

The Datastar wire protocol is based on the SSE response format, where each event contains an (optional) event: entry and one or more data: entries. Distinct events are separated by double newline characters (\n\n). In this case, we’re sending a datastar-patch-signals event that tells the browser to update signal values. The patched values are expressed as a JSON object where the keys correspond to signal names and the values correspond to the signal values.

You can look at this example on a separate page, but for the sake of convenience I’ll go ahead and embed it right here:

Although this is a very simple example, look at all the things we’re not doing 😜: we don’t need to set up an EventSource object, or use fetch to start the SSE connection on the client side, we don’t need to go through the DOM and update anything that’s bound to the $time signal. On the server side we just stream changes to the server state to the client (eventually though, we might want to introduce some abstractions for sending a datastar-patch-signals event or other types of events, but this is pretty trivial…)

Let’s look at how signals are handled in Datastar a bit more closely. I’ve been playing with Datastar in the last few days and have observed the some peculiarities:

In Datastar, signals are global to the page. They can’t be scoped to a part of the DOM, but they can be namespaced by nesting them inside objects:

Alternatively, you can use the following notation, handy when you have key values that contain slashes, or other special characters:

By default, Datastar will send all signal values back to the server on every user action, which may be problematic if you have lots of signals on your page. In order to prevent signal values from being sent to the server on each request, the signal name must begin with an underscore.

Finally, an important aspect of Datastar signals (and indeed, Datastar in general,) is that Datastar doesn’t really have a Javascript API. You can’t just access signal values from Javascript (this is by design), which may make it harder to integrate Datastar with other tools. But there is a workaround for that and it’s pretty simple:

#9923. Anthropic-Themed Phishing Emails Bypass Top Security Tools

Obvious phishing emails with numerous red flags are somehow getting past some of the industry-leading secure email gateway (SEG) products.

Attackers are managing to sneak low-grade phishing emails through brand name email security products, as evidenced by a recent Anthropic impersonation campaign.

The campaign, described in a new blog post by Cofense, won't impress anybody. Since September, an unidentified threat actor has been sending out emails around the world, pretending to grant early access to Anthropic's cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) technology. Their goal: stealing Google and Microsoft account credentials.

To avoid being relegated to spam folders, the attacker has been using novice tactics: shortening their malicious URLs, adding CAPTCHAs to their phishing flow, and leveraging legitimate video conferencing tools. The only remarkable thing about the campaign, really, is that it actually seems to be working.

Even as far as phishing campaigns go, this one's pretty lazy.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

Attackers are appealing to targets with VIP invites to a "private preview" of Anthropic's supposed "new social media AI tool." Emails emphasize that this special early look is "private, invitation-only."

Right off the bat, there are ample reasons to be suspicious. The email titles have a grammatical error. The email sender's name includes a typo — "Austin from nthropic" — and their domain belongs to GoTo Webinar, not Anthropic. Visually, the messages are barebones, possessing no visual elements that even attempt to impersonate Anthropic branding.

If for some reason someone actually clicks on the fake registration link — a link that doesn't point to an Anthropic or even a conferencing app domain — they'll end up on a fake Zoom meeting page. If, further, the victim doesn't catch that a GoTo Webinar invite led to a Zoom call, they might choose to sign into Zoom via Google or Microsoft Single-Sign On (SSO). If they choose Google, they won't even be prompted for a password, thus making half of this malicious campaign completely useless, even to the attacker running it.

Inconsistent brand impersonations and missing or broken data theft flows are endemic to AI-generated campaigns; Cofense couldn't confirm if AI was used here. "However, due to the multiple variations of Zoom pages, it's likely generative AI was used," Cofense researcher Jacob Malimban says.

He points to one bit of additional evidence: Beginning Oct. 28, the threat actor began spoofing Anthropic's website instead of Zoom's. The similar but slightly off format of the Anthropic spoofing page, he says, also suggests AI generation.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

The overall package is so maladroit that one can only wonder how such an email bypassed any spam filter in the first place. In fact, Cofense found these emails getting through market-leading email security products like the Proofpoint Secure Email Gateway (SEG) and Microsoft Defender for Office 365. Cofense pointed to a few little details that might help explain why.

First, the emails are sent from a legitimate email address, customercare@gotowebinar[.]com — a shared sender address that any GoTo Webinar user might use to distribute webinar information. The legitimacy and ubiquity of this shared address shields the sender from scrutiny.

Second, the malicious registration link in the emails was run through a URL shortener, Zapier, eliminating a security product's ability to interpret red flags in the domain itself.

Lastly, the phishing flow incorporates two separate CAPTCHAs. The first — a Cloudflare CAPTCHA, presented before the fake Zoom or Anthropic page — is meant to stop an automated scanner in its tracks.

The second CAPTCHA — placed between the fake Zoom or Anthropic page and the fake SSO page — is a malicious twist on the form, designed to block VPN services, Tor browsers, and other tools defenders might use. "Some phish kits used that specific type of CAPTCHA before. It appears to have been actively developed by threat actors to detect the tools of both automated and human activity, as well as see if the IP address was proxied," Malimban explains.

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

None of these tactics will knock anyone's socks off but, in the gestalt, they seem to do the trick.

"The reality of modern cybersecurity is that Secure Email Gateways (SEGs) will always have blind spots," he says.

Barney adds that organizations should assume phishing emails will end up in employees' email inboxes, and therefore security teams need to build defenses that focus on identity.

"If an employee is tricked by a fake Anthropic lure and their Microsoft or Google credentials are compromised, strict least-privilege access policies, phishing-resistant multifactor authentication and privileged access management are what prevent the attacker from moving laterally, elevating privileges and accessing sensitive data," he advises. Lastly, he adds, "Utilizing a centralized password manager that validates domain URLs before autofilling credentials provides a critical last line of defense against the lookalike domains used in this attack, neutralizing the threat at the point of interaction."

In the spirit of Cybersecurity Awareness Month 2026, and its emphasis on avoiding and reporting phishing scams, Malimban adds, "We hope that employees are trained using Secure Behavior Management to recognize and report phishing. To defend against suspicious account access, organizations should have robust account monitoring, like with CISA's free tool (Logging Made Easy). All in all, having multiple controls and defense in depth is necessary to defend against modern attacks."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

User namespaces are a key part of the kernel's toolkit for assembling containers; processes within a user namespace can appear to have full root access to the system while gaining no extra privileges in the wider system. At least, that is the intent. In practice, keeping privilege contained within a user namespace has often turned out to be difficult. As an example, consider this small patch series from Josef Bacik, which is intended to address some situations where a process within a user namespace can elevate the privileges of processes outside of it.

#9921. Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern shows up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

This is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

ProvenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

The verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a new setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

We tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts said 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an important area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This shows it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

That adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval says "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the issue well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;

Like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

However, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

#9920. As Russia's Cyberwar Evolves, Belarus Steps Forward

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The "FrostyNeighbor" advanced persistent threat (APT) launched a destructive attack in Ukraine and is raising concerns about deeper alignment with Russian cyber objectives.

Researchers have spotted the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned threat actor against a critical target in Ukraine, suggesting Belarus may be upping its support for Russian national objectives — carrying implications for much of Europe.

ESET this week published its APT Activity Report for Q2 and Q3 2026. The report highlights a range of state-sponsored activity across Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, but one of the most significant assertions involves Belarus, an Eastern European country that has been close allies with Russia in the latter's invasion of Ukraine.

Historically, Belarusian cyber operations have been tracked separately from those attributed directly to Russian intelligence services, though researchers have long observed overlap in targeting and strategic interests. The Belarusan state-affiliated group FrostyNeighbor — also tracked as UNC1151 — has been known for disinformation and cyber espionage, the latter conducted through various means such as spear phishing and malware.

Related:Russia's Hybrid Cyber-Physical War in Europe Heats Up

While the Eastern European country has also set its sights on Ukrainian and Polish targets in phishing attacks to further its own and possibly Russia's goals, ESET identified a recent escalation in these activities. Mainly, ESET's report notes that its researchers "identified the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned threat actor that we have documented in the European theater."

Specifically, FrostyNeighbor deployed Chisel, UltraVNC, Cobalt Strike, and a VBScript wiper via Group Policy against a manufacturing company in Ukraine that ESET said "plays an important role in the country's transportation sector," which is notable because destructive operations up until this point have been explicitly Russia-aligned.

"While some of their targeting interests overlap, notably around the drone sector, our telemetry more clearly points to Belarus-aligned groups acting as cyberproxies or force multipliers for Russia," the report read. "We observed increased and more assertive activity from Belarus-aligned threat actors, with their operations increasingly reflecting Russia’s intelligence priorities in Ukraine in some areas."

Damien Schaeffer, senior malware researcher at ESET, says that the strongest evidence for an increasing operational closeness with Russia is the number of attacks and the victimology that appears closer to and aligned with Russia's strategic priorities than Belarus's own, as well as a sophistication behind these attacks, "which seems relatively high to Belarus's potential interests alone." He says ESET first observed this trend of increasing aggressiveness at the beginning of 2024.

This comes as North Korea expands its own military cooperation with Russia in the latter's war on Ukraine, which ESET added could mean cyber activity will continue to align as well.

Russia's war on Ukraine stretches far beyond Ukraine, especially in the realm of cyber operations. Russia has grown bolder in cyberattacks particularly against European countries that support Ukraine militarily or politically, are on NATO's eastern flank, and support critical logistics hubs for aid flowing into Ukraine.

This, to varying degrees, has included Poland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Sweden, Czech Republic, and Germany, among others. In other words, if Russian allies are growing bolder in their cyberactivities explicitly supporting Russia, that carries consequences for all of Europe.

Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at Recorded Future, tells Dark Reading that its evidence shows FrostyNeighbor as an actor executing sustained operations and evolving its techniques, though not necessarily an overall increase in operational scale nor shared operational command.

Recorded Future's recommendation is to explicitly track Belarus-linked clusters and correlate their infrastructure, tools, and targeting with Russian threat campaigns "while preserving attribution distinctions."

"Threat models should cover credential theft, persistent access, and the use of compromised accounts to reach additional people. Intelligence collection should include malicious login infrastructure, email exploitation, personal-account targeting, and abuse of trusted contacts, which are the access routes documented in these campaigns," Leslie says. "Defenders do not need proof of Russian tasking to prioritize an actor already targeting them."

While researchers differ on whether Belarusian activity represents deeper operational integration with Russia, they appear to agree that defenders should not dismiss Belarus-linked actors as secondary threats. As Leslie explains, CERT Polska in June 2026 identified UNC1151 as one of the most active APT groups it monitors, "observing new phishing domains almost daily in the preceding weeks."

Organizations in sectors tied to government, transportation, and defense that show support for Ukraine may increasingly encounter campaigns whose objectives align closely with Moscow's broader strategic interests.

#9919. Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

The pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀

Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:

These arenas compare models by presenting users with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

While human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously said by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡

Importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

Numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an important gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

You can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

The “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is important for voice agents and other interactive apps.

For streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

The default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

The goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

We will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Issues and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗

Compare and rank TTS voice models with blind A/B voting

Explore speech model performance across datasets

TTS systems evaluated on objective metrics.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

The check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS."

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

Open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let users listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

Human feedback remains an important part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as new TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and users better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

GitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard

#9917. Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

A security firm patched a decade-old app to prevent the takeover of millions of machines, highlighting that abandoned domains remain a boon to attackers.

When managed security service provider Eye Security spotted an odd update process in a client's telemetry that appeared to be reaching out to outdated — and in some cases, malicious — domains, the company decided to take a deeper look.

The updater belonged to a modified version of Time4Popcorn, a 2014-era BitTorrent client that allows movies to be downloaded from the Internet, and even after a decade, the persistent updater continued to run on more than 2.5 million Windows machines and an estimated 300,000 Macs, checking for new software, according to the MSSP's advisory. The problem: Many of the domains checked by the updater were open to registration, which could allow any would-be cyberattacker to register the domain and have an easy way to place software on millions of machines.

The situation highlights the issue of old infrastructure and the threat it poses to users and businesses, especially if the business's employees work from home, Niels Teusink, principal security researcher for Eye Security, wrote in the analysis.

Related:Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

"[W]hile these users chose to install Popcorn Time, none of them chose to have a forgotten updater running in the background for years, ready to run any code with full privileges for whoever controlled one of its domains," the company stated in its advisory. "With millions of systems affected and the software long abandoned, there was no vendor to fix this and no patch on the way: if we didn't act, nobody would."

The risk of domains that are dropped by a legitimate service and then picked up again, or bought by a gray-market or criminal operator — sometimes called "dropcatch domains" — have become an increasing issue as developers have stopped updating, or sold off, legacy software infrastructure. In February 2025, for example, exposure management firm watchTowr discovered 150 Amazon S3 buckets that had been abandoned, so they registered and found that more than 8 million HTTP requests from government and companies came in for resources that had been hosted at those addresses.

And with AI enabling a more sophisticated analysis of software projects, attackers may be able to more quickly do the necessary research to find domains that could be a backdoor into users' systems, says Benjamin Harris, founder and CEO of watchTowr.

"AI is definitely driving the barrier-to-entry down for this kind of research very quickly," he says. "We're seeing AI used to reproduce vulnerabilities, find zero days, but applied to this, AI can be used to install a bunch of software, install network taps, see what all the software reaches out to, see what's not registered, or see what's been abandoned and what we can hijack."

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

Typically, there are two types of vulnerable domains that questionable operators might take an interest in. The first are homograph domains that look like their legitimate cousins and include both typosquatting domains, such as "gmai[.]com," that try to catch browsers whose users mistyped a URL, and lookalike domains that are used in phishing to visually fool users. The value of these types of domains to the owner varies, depending on the amount of traffic they attract, says Renée Burton, vice president of threat intelligence at cybersecurity vendor Infoblox.

However, dropcatch domains that are integrated into the supply chain for a piece of software are a completely different — and more serious — risk, she says. Infoblox has registered hundreds of domains that had been part of supply chains to prevent attackers from using them.

"Supply chain attacks can happen at a moment's notice, and depending on how dropped domains are integrated into existing software, a threat actor can quickly abuse a supply chain dropped domain to conduct sophisticated attacks that lead to data loss and ransomware," Burton says.

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

In 2024, Chinese company Funnull bought the polyfill[.]io domain from the creator of the Polyfill service and began redirecting users to tens of thousands of websites.

The Popcorn Time issue highlights the problem. Anyone with access to the domains, and with some reverse engineering, could figure out how to tinker with the legacy updaters. In fact, that's what Eye Security did, updating the code to stop the automated process of reaching out to the old domains.

"All we needed to do was supply a link to an executable and the program would download it and then execute it with high privileges (NT AUTHORITYSYSTEM)," Teusink wrote. "There was no code signing and this process was all happening over HTTP."

Eye Security stressed that another project, confusingly also named Popcorn Time, is a 2025 effort to create a legitimate streaming service and is not impacted by the legacy update issues.

Companies should know the domains that their employees are reaching out to and the reputation of those domains, and should extend that monitoring and protection to remote users, says watchTowr's Harris.

"The big challenge with things like BYOD and working from home is that now the network perimeter extends from not just your corporate network ... but the user's home network as well," he says.

The community needs to come together as well, says Infoblox's Burton. While taking active defense to the same extent as Eye Security continues to be legally problematic, finding legacy and unused infrastructure is something that security communities on the Internet can continue to work on, she says.

"Threat actors understand the value of controlling a domain which is integrated into an existing supply chain and being queried by real people on a regular basis," Burton says. "We need more defenders looking for proactive ways to disrupt domain drop schemes by purchasing high-value pending drop domains before threat actors, and by looking for ways to reduce threat actors cash out opportunities from these attacks."

(plaintext version for nerds - patches welcome)

So, last time I wrote about account takeover using XSS on the CI platform of SourceHut.

This time I found something not nearly as ‘impactful’, but still interesting. Sorry for taking this long, but my SSD literally died1 and while waiting for a warranty repair I had to buy a used one (have you seen the prices yet??)2. It finally arrived so here I am.

So, if you want me to work faster, just drop me some money.3

Again, as you might know, I am not very excited about the current wave of natural language processing.4

No NLP has been used in this research. The mistakes are all mine.

SourceHut has been undergoing quite an architectural change. Its frontend was first built using Flask and Jinja templates and SQLAlchemy. But, for performance reasons, and for other reasons (decoupling of business logic, graphql) the API has been ported over to Go.

Back in 2021, while moving registration code from the frontend to the graphql backend, a subtle logic bug got introduced. While the frontend never shows a registration form, and states prominently ‘registration is currently closed’, the form handler is still there. It correctly states that registration is closed on every error path, but on the happy path it does not seem to ever check it. So if you happen to remember how to submit the form…

You just need to POST /register/step2 with your desired username, email and password. If the server in question disables registration, but has its SMTP configured properly (you still need to do email confirmation), boom, you are in.

There is no registration form displayed, so there is no token. However, fortunately for us attackers, the token from /login works just fine.

Does anyone know a bug bounty program where the researcher pays an upfront participation fee? I will set mine up this way for sure, and you should consider it too, if you are drowning in submissions.
