InfoQ Homepage News Google Cloud API Gateway Introduces Streaming Support for Real-Time and AI-Powered Applications

Nov 05, 2026 2 min read

Google has announced the public preview of streaming support for API Gateway, extending its traditional request-response model to support applications requiring real-time communication. According to Google, this is particularly relevant for AI applications that provide streaming model responses, multi-step agent workflows, and interactive sessions.

The new functionality enables streaming endpoints to operate behind API Gateway while retaining existing gateway policies and security controls, thereby addressing a previous limitation:

Until now, developers building those experiences in API Gateway had to make an uncomfortable choice: put API Gateway in front of their APIs and give up streaming, or route streaming endpoints around the gateway and give up the authentication, API key enforcement, and observability that made the gateway essential in the first place.

API Gateway supports several streaming patterns, including Server-Sent Events (SSE), chunked transfer encoding and HTTP response streaming, WebSockets, and gRPC. Streaming connections can remain open for up to one hour, after which clients must establish a new connection if continued communication is required.

The new release introduces streaming support without requiring changes to existing API specifications or the use of specific APIs, extensions, or annotations. Google emphasizes that all existing API configurations and capabilities continue to work as before, including API key enforcement, JWT validation, service account authentication to backends, Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring integration, and path templating and request routing.

Another benefit of the new release is the introduction of predictable gateway hostnames. Previously, gateway hostnames included a generated hash and could only be determined after the gateway had been created. Now, they follow a deterministic format: GATEWAY_ID-PROJECT_NUMBER.REGION.gateway.dev, allowing developers to reference and configure them before creating the resource.

Google highlights the importance of streaming support for AI applications, where model responses are generated progressively rather than delivered as a single, complete response. Using the new functionality, developers will be able to stream model responses in real time, update agent progress during multi-step tasks, support tool-calling protocols and connections to remote MCP servers, and handle interactive AI applications.

API Gateway also supports model routing, providing a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint to route requests to Gemini, Claude, or OpenAI gpt-oss models based on the model field in the request payload.

Model routing plus streaming means clients get a familiar, standards-based streaming interface, while you retain centralized control over which models are reachable, by whom, and under what policy.

Commenting on Google's announcement, X user emildrops highlights two important limitations. First, "existing gateways can't be switched in place" and, second, "latency measures the whole stream, not time to first byte... so latency graphs will look broken for reasons that aren't bugs". Similarly, LinkedIn user Ehsan Elahi Zaheer points out that:

Monitoring also needs care: gateway request-latency metrics measure stream duration, not time to first byte. A single latency chart can hide very different user experiences.

During the preview period, developers must explicitly enable the new functionality by specifying the --enable-streaming command-line flag when creating a gateway.

#9897. Declarative Dragging

Joshua Horowitz, Andrew Blinn, Jeffrey Heer

What if making a diagram draggable was as simple as specifying what it can become?

Drag-and-drop makes the digital graspable. But designing bespoke drag interactions involves a lot of fiddly code to handle geometry, feedback, and animations. As a result, many people, from educators to game designers, mathematicians to creative tool builders, often don't bother.

Declarative dragging inverts the problem. Rather than programming all that visual behavior directly, you simply say, for each element you want to make draggable, which future states of your application dragging it should lead to. Our system speculatively renders those states to work out where things can go, then combines these possible worlds into a smooth, responsive drag-and-drop interaction.

Our goal with this project is to let people keep working within the semantic worlds they inhabit, while helping them turn the rules of their worlds into rich tactile interactions in ours.

A five-minute video introducing declarative dragging.

D2 is model-driven: An interface author makes an element draggable by specifying which future model states should be accessible by dragging it. An engine speculatively renders these states to view trees, extracts the position of the dragged element in each of these renderings, and uses these to synthesize a drag-and-drop interaction, all without detailed work required by the interface author.

To provide greater expressive range and customizability, D2 is composable: simple model-driven drag-and-drop behaviors can be combined to create more complex ones, and modifiers can layer features like floating, snapping, and transitions. For more details, see the paper.

We implemented D2 in a library called Dragology, built for SVG interfaces on the web.

See our demo gallery for many more interactives built with Dragology.

Josh has been working on a variety of new, more intricate mathematical explorables. We've found Dragology particularly suited to interfaces that combine parallel representations, where you see the same system from different perspectives. In the permutation lab below, interacting with any one representation fluidly updates the others, even halfway through a drag, showing their relationships in real time.

Andrew has been working to bring declarative dragging to existing applications, including his research on user interfaces for programming languages, as well as restarting work on the math game concept that kicked it all off.

#9896. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

#9894. PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Organizations in the region face growing cyberattacks from the known India-linked threat group, which leverages legitimate Windows functionality in three distinct attack chains.

A known South Asian cyber-espionage group has been targeting organizations across the region with attacks designed to compromise Windows systems, establish persistence, and give attackers remote control over infected machines using custom malware.

The attacks, attributed "with high confidence" to the South Asian threat group known as Bitter (aka TA397), involve three distinct infection chains and demonstrate the group's expanding malware capabilities, according to new research from FortiGuard Labs published today.

Bitter, one of several threat groups linked to India, has been active since at least 2013 and has historically targeted government, energy, and engineering organizations. The group is known for using tailored attack campaigns to gain persistent access to victim networks, collect information, and maintain remote control over compromised systems.

At the center of the latest threat campaign is PapRAT, a custom remote access Trojan (RAT) that gives attackers extensive control over compromised Windows systems, including the ability to execute commands, manipulate files, capture screenshots, and download additional payloads, according to FortiGuard Labs.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

"This campaign illustrates how Bitter combines native Windows tools with custom malware to establish and maintain access to targeted systems," Cara Lin, a FortiGuard Labs threat researcher, wrote in the post.

Bitter has recently revamped PapRAT from a C++ code base to Rust, expanding its functionality in the process from eight commands to 11, according to the report. Additional capabilities in the latest version include PowerShell execution, a sleep directive, and a clean-exit command.

"PapRAT's C++ and Rust implementations indicate continued investment in Bitter's toolset," Lin wrote.

Indeed, attackers have increasingly adopted Rust for malware development for various reasons, including its cross-platform development capabilities and potential evasion advantages.

The latest updates to PapRAT also underscore the importance of certain defensive measures, including "monitoring malicious behavior across scripting tools, scheduled tasks, and installer activity alongside detecting known malware signatures," Lin wrote.

Researchers observed three distinct attack chains being used by Bitter, all of which exploit legitimate Windows functionality to disguise malicious behavior.

These tactics demonstrate "how advanced cyberespionage operations deliberately abuse native system tools to evade traditional endpoint detection," notes Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

The first attack chain uses a malicious LNK file that abuses the native Windows ftp.exe utility to execute scripts and create scheduled tasks that maintain contact with the attackers' command-and-control (C2) server.

The second uses a VHDX disk image containing an LNK file that opens a decoy spreadsheet while silently launching an MSI installer to deploy PapRAT.

The third attack begins with a URL shortcut that retrieves an LNK file through WebDAV, leading to an MSI installer that deploys PapRAT. In this chain, PapRAT also delivers WmRAT, a secondary implant previously documented by other researchers, according to FortiGuard Labs.

"By co-opting native Windows utilities like ftp.exe and scheduled tasks to establish initial command-and-control communication, threat actors operate within trusted administrative channels before deploying custom malware," Barney observes. "When an intrusion leverages trusted system processes, signature-based controls simply have nothing to alert on."

This so-called "hybrid tradecraft," which combines legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware, requires organizations to focus on strict privilege boundaries and identity security rather than relying on endpoint signatures alone as part of a comprehensive defense strategy, Barney says.

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

To defend against these attacks, organizations should treat unexpected LNK files, URL shortcuts, disk images, and MSI packages with caution, particularly when delivered through unsolicited messages, Lin recommended in the post.

"Combining user awareness with controls that detect suspicious execution chains and outbound C2 traffic can help limit exposure to campaigns that blend legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware," she wrote.

The third attack chain is particularly problematic for defenders because removing PapRAT from compromised systems may not eliminate the attacker's access, observes Jason Soroko, senior fellow at Sectigo.

This means defenders need to look deeper into their systems "to check what else was installed and identify scripts and scheduled tasks that could keep fetching commands," he says. A comprehensive recovery effort must look beyond the file that triggered the original alert to identify any additional payloads, persistence mechanisms, or other components of the compromise.

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9893. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

Built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎

#9892. Software Line Specialist

This is a code-only role; for AI-native jobs, please look at our other listings

We’re looking for a senior software line specialist, in TypeScript!

ACME Inc. is a fast-growing startup helping small businesses monitor their financials. We work with business owners across the globe, turning their feedback into actionable insights. Backed by Maltese Falcon Capital, we recently raised a $15M Series A to bring effortless monitoring to every brick-and-mortar store.

You’ll be joining a high-performance, close-knit team of AI natives! We’ve been AI-first for the past 2 years, with every part of the product agent-friendly and interconnected: design, development, QA, CI/CD, infra, data analysis. We like to say that our stack is English!

While English has gotten us 99.5% of the way there, we’re in need of a hands-on engineer ready to close the final 0.5%. Over time, we’ve noticed some issues that are immune to prompts and catch agents in loops. Sometimes, the issue at hand gets fixed, but it results in another issue. This is where you step in. As a line specialist, your job will be to investigate and fix complex issues, primarily by reading the underlying code.

We’re looking for someone ready to open an IDE and dive deep into an unknown codebase — a fearless detective who is comfortable inspecting logs and database rows, and has the know-how to piece all the information together. The perfect candidate should be willing to work on a problem for hours, sometimes even days.

This is a new position for us. We expect someone who works autonomously, makes sound decisions independently and takes full ownership of their work. We are happy to help in any way we can (you’ll have access to agents’ reasoning traces), but ultimately we depend on your confidence in understanding the problem and shipping a solution.

We feel it prudent to point out that you will be allowed to work on one thing at a time in this role. While parallel development is the default, we understand line specialists prefer to tackle problems in a single-threaded manner, so we will do our best to provide a distraction-free environment for your best work.

To be clear, this role does not include feature development. You’re welcome to look at our AI-native listings if you have more interest in such work!

#9890. Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

The latest "Digital Defense Report" identifies government agencies as prime targets for AI attacks but doesn't mention that they are broadly being targeted through Microsoft bugs.

AI is changing cybersecurity. The hope is that software will eventually ship with fewer vulnerabilities, while the expectation in the meantime is that vendors will issue eye-popping volumes of software patches as a result of using AI to identify flaws in existing products. Software customers will increasingly use AI to more effectively and efficiently protect their networks. These promising developments will take time to unfold, as vendors and their customers learn how to incorporate AI into their software development and cybersecurity risk management workflows.

Attackers, meanwhile, are already using AI to generate novel attacks and orchestrate increasingly complex and large-scale hacking campaigns. AI is already enabling criminal groups to achieve hacking successes normally reserved for patient, highly resourced nation-state threat actors. And nation-state threat actors are using AI to increase the scale and sophistication of their cyber operations. The threat level is rising at an alarming rate.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

Microsoft flagged the impacts of AI on cybersecurity in its recently released "2026 Digital Defense Report." Among its findings, it assessed that government agencies and services were the most affected by cyber threats and frequently targeted for nation-state activity.

Microsoft's report has a major blind spot, however: the impact of legacy software, especially its own, on organizations' cyber-risk. Legacy software will remain the substrate of organizations' attack surface for the foreseeable future. Vendors need to up their security game, and their customers need to demand better security from their vendors, particularly as AI heightens the threat landscape.

For example, with an 85% market share, Microsoft is the most dominant player in the US public sector productivity software market. Its products are therefore a prime target for state-sponsored groups seeking access to US government agencies and the data and secrets they are charged with protecting. So we should expect attackers to prize vulnerabilities in Microsoft's products and devote a substantial proportion of their hacking efforts to these popular products.

But there is more to the story than Microsoft's sheer prevalence in federal IT. Microsoft's grip on the federal IT market exposes the US government to a disproportionate share of cyber vulnerabilities. According to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Microsoft accounts for nearly 16% of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) so far this year — the most of any company. Microsoft accounts for nearly 23% of known exploited vulnerabilities from November 2021 (when CISA began tracking KEVs) to October 2026.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

By comparison, the next-highest vendor, Cisco, is responsible for approximately 7% in 2026 and 6% total, less than half of Microsoft's share.

Some agencies even rely on Microsoft as their single software vendor. This isn't particularly surprising — Microsoft has a track record of locking customers into its ecosystem by bundling its cloud computing offerings with office and security products (bundling is one area of focus of the Federal Trade Commission’s ongoing antitrust investigation into Microsoft) and then making it too difficult or costly for customers to switch vendors.

In 2023, the US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) discontinued its Data Loss Prevention program after moving to bundle security tools into a sole-source Microsoft enterprise license. The move reportedly put 18 million veterans' personal records at risk of leakage. The VA has now moved to reverse course by seeking alternatives to Microsoft, having recognized the consequences of a Microsoft monoculture. Lesson learned.

Related:PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Microsoft's Digital Defense Report identifies how frequently government agencies are affected by cyber threats and targeted for nation-state activity. Microsoft knows this firsthand. Since 2023, Chinese state-sponsored actors have compromised Microsoft products in at least two significant instances, accessing over two dozen US government agencies' emails in one attack and compromising at least seven agencies in another in July 2025.

Russian state-backed actors have also exploited Microsoft's weak security at least three times since 2020, including the infamous SolarWinds attack and an operation to exfiltrate emails between Microsoft personnel and government agencies. US government officials and advisory bodies have concluded that these breaches were preventable and caused by Microsoft's negligence. The reach and severity of breaches will only grow as China, Russia, and other nation-state threat actors become AI-native and AI tools become increasingly sophisticated.

Microsoft deserves some credit for using AI to evaluate products it has already deployed: its record-setting Patch Tuesday count of 974 vulnerabilities disclosed last month is no doubt the result of using AI to identify flaws. But that's not good enough.

All software vendors, including Microsoft, should invest more in the security of their products before they are released, even if it comes at the expense of slowing the rollout of new product features. And they should all be transparent to customers about these processes to enable customers to make more informed purchasing decisions. Otherwise, Microsoft's "2027 Digital Defense Report" will paint an even darker picture of the threat environment.

Director of the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance, Stanford University

Andrew Grotto founded and directs the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance at Stanford University's Center for International Security and Cooperation. He serves as the faculty lead for the Cyber Policy and Security specialization in Stanford’s master’s in international policy program, where he teaches courses on cyber policy and economic statecraft. He is also a visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution. Previously, he was senior advisor to the Secretary of Commerce for technology policy during the Obama administration and Senior Director for Cyber Policy on the National Security Council in the Obama and Trump administrations. He advises technology companies on digital risks, including companies that compete with Microsoft.

The egui.rs demo now works as expected with --pref dom._webegpu_enabled.

We’re interested to hear how well your favourite websites run in Servo! Report successes in this Zulip thread or this Github discussion, and failures in our GitHub issues.

Our accessibility tree (--pref accessibility_enabled) now reports geometry bounds for inline elements (@alice, #47905) and does much less work when responding to DOM changes (@alice, @mrobinson, #47690). Additionally, elements with display: none are reported as hidden (@alice, #47772).

We had lots of conformance improvements for our WebGL2 implementation (--pref dom_webgl2_enabled) (@mxmgorin, #48423, #48441, #48470, #48479, #48495, #48473, #48536).

Support for WSIWYG editors (which rely heavily on contenteditable) is going very well: keyboard inputs are now hooked up when --pref dom_exec_command_enabled is present, so many editors are now usable (example).

Closed captioning for video elements is making progress. Text tracks now fire enter, exit, and cuechange events (@TimvdLippe, #47725). Media elements now return the full sorted list of text tracks (@TimvdLippe, #47785), and adding cues to a text track now sets that track correctly (@TimvdLippe, #48012). Text track objects now reflect the attributes of the associated element. Text track URLs are fetched at the correct time (@TimvdLippe, #48325), and active cues are computed correctly (@TimvdLippe, #48305), while text track cues are ordered as expected (@TimvdLippe, #48368). Additionally, WebVTT parsing can now recover from errors (@TimvdLippe, #48391).

The Sanitizer API (--pref dom_sanitizer_enabled) now accepts the javascriptURLs property (@skyz1, #47867).

IndexedDB continues to improve: tables no longer error if unrelated tables contain duplicate index names (--pref dom_indexeddb_enabled) (@leowatts, #47936). Additionally, we implemented openCursor() and openKeyCursor() on IDBIndex (@kuntal-devrat, #48281), as well as advance(), continue(), and continuePrimaryKey() on IDBCursor (@kuntal-devrat, #48400).

We implemented the getTimeline() and setTimeline() methods for the Animation interface (--pref dom_web_animations_enabled) (@simonwuelker, #48122).

There’s a new API for events originating from accessibility tools: Servo::forward_accessibility_action (@alice, @mrobinson, #48512).

There is also an API to clear session history: WebView::clear_session_history (@Narfinger, #47483).

The WebView::set_throttled API has been removed (@mrobinson, #39923). Throttling automatically occurs when a WebView is hidden and is stopped when shown.

The WebViewDelegate::notify_focus_changed method was removed, along with the Servo methods focus and blur (@mrobinson, #48364). Embedders must call WebView::set_focused whenever a WebView has gained or lost system focus.

The webgl feature has been added to the default_web_features feature (@janeoa, #47866). If an embedding does not want to ship with WebGL support they will now need to disable default features.

Multiprocess mode is enabled at build time with the new Cargo feature multprocess (@Narfinger, #47360). To remove support for this feature (reducing binary size by ~2MB), build Servo with default features disabled.

Two new preferences exist to tune garbage collector behaviour: js_mem_gc_malloc_threshold_base_mb and js_mem_gc_urgent_threshold_mb (@mxmgorin, #47999). These can help on memory-constrained devices, and more information is available in the SpiderMonkey source (base, urgent).

The JVM compatibility target was raised to 11 on Android (@veyndan, #48414).

It is now possible to cross-compile the OpenHarmony build from Windows hosts (@jschwe, #48392).

Unhandled promise rejections are reported to the JS console (@TTyChud, #48486), making it easier to narrow down web compatibility issues in Servo.

The OpenHarmony SDK was updated to API level 23 (@Narfinger, #48505).

Pressing Control+A (or Command+A on macOS) now selects all the content in a document (@dzfrias, @mrobinson, #48025). It is no longer possible to copy text inside of password inputs (@dzfrias, #48404).

Embedder-originating JS (e.g. devtools console or embedding APIs) will always execute, even in documents that disable scripting via sandboxing or CSP (@derdilla, #48394).

We improved performance by removing unnecessary allocations (@Narfinger, @TimvdLippe, @yezhizhen, #47689, #47839, #47838, #47982, #48006, #48036, #48099, #48204, #48127, #48218, #48357, #48386, #48422, #48440, #48452, #48508), preallocating more when building vectors (@jschwe, @Narfinger, @sagudev, @webbeef, #47455, #47613, #48026, #48398), and avoiding IPC in single process mode (@leowatts, @Narfinger, @Uiniel, @TTyChud, #47691, #47718, #48002, #48073, #48476, #48435).

We also sped up Servo by reducing interactions with the GC (@TimvdLippe, @Narfinger, #47818, #48257, #48396), and doing less work when modifying selections (@SimonSapin, #47579), dispatching events (@webbeef, #48078), calculating font metrics (@RichardTjokroutomo, #48238), and indexing window frames (@mrobinson, #47832).

We reduced memory usage in common cases by reusing buffers (@Narfinger, #47751), clearing more page-specific data (@Radeonares32, @Narfinger, @jschwe, @mrobinson, @mxmgorin, #47651, #47806, #47805, #48166, #48295, #48297, #48016), compacting data structures (@Narfinger, @webbeef, @SimonSapin, @mrobinson, #47776, #48039, #48050, #47742, #48301, #48296, #48105), and sharing more buffers (@jdm, #47998). We also fixed a memory leak involving

We turned on thread affinity boosting on Linux, which can improve performance on some CPU architectures (@jschwe, #47058).

We’re working on statically preventing a footgun that can lead to uncollectible GC cycles and leaking memory (@Gae24, @jdm, @lumiscosity, @SilvioPilato, @sahilnyk, @TTyChud, @kuntal-devrat, @MohamedAli00949, #47941, #48013, #48021, #48035, #48033, #48051, #48072, #48171, #48209, #48248, #48246, #48264, #48285, #48311, #48408, #48053, #48156, #48186, #48223, #48315, #47872, #47698, #47682, #47735, #47816, #47817, #47794, #47909, #47934, #47935, #47954, #48022, #47955, #48058, #48228, #48247, #48261, #48280, #48302, #48316, #48328, #48346, #48355, #48262, #48377, #48304, #48378, #48388, #48432).

We fixed panics in WebRTC (@MunishMummadi, #4772), execCommand() on Document (@TimvdLippe, #47784),
